articles.title: Satellite radar tech startup Kapta Space raises $24M from Bill Gates-backed fund and defense investors
articles.author: John Cook
paras: Kapta Space , a Seattle startup building lower-cost, steerable radar sensors for satellites, has raised $24 million in a Series A funding round to scale production and meet growing demand for defense intelligence contracts.

The investment brings total funding to $30 million, following an initial $5 million seed round led by MetaVC — a metamaterials-focused fund backed by Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates and former Microsoft executive Nathan Myhrvold . It also previously received a $1.8 million grant from the Department of Defense.

The deal highlights the ongoing momentum in the Pacific Northwest’s commercial space ecosystem, where a growing cluster of venture-backed startups is building hardware alongside major satellite operations like SpaceX’s Starlink facility in Redmond and Amazon’s Leo constellation program.

Founded in 2023 by CEO Milton Perque and Adam Bily, Kapta uses metamaterials for its proprietary Metamaterial Electronically Scanned Array (MESA) architecture. The tech provides high-resolution, geospatial imagery and ground-target tracking without the extreme cost, power demands, and manufacturing complexity of traditional systems.

Both founders bring deep local expertise to the hardware: Perque and Bily were previously engineering leaders at radar maker Echodyne. Perque’s background also includes stops at Metacept and Intellectual Ventures, while Bily served as an antenna engineer at Apple and satellite startup Astranis.
The fresh capital will help Kapta expand manufacturing, qualify its hardware for spaceflight, and prepare for initial orbital demonstration missions.

Kapta’s software-defined architecture aims to make persistent satellite tracking feasible at constellation scale, letting spacecraft rapidly steer beams to continuously detect and hold custody of moving targets across air, sea and land.

“The mission calls for persistent awareness, and that requires us to rethink how radar has to work at constellation scale,” said Milton Perque, Founder and CEO of Kapta Space, in a release . “Traditional architectures are cost-prohibitive and were never designed for the scale these missions now demand.”

Washington Harbour Partners, which specializes in defense tech investing, led the round, with Bison Ventures co-leading. Previous backer MetaVC Partners joined alongside MYDA Capital, Entrada Ventures, Aurelia Foundry, and Fitz Gate Ventures.

“Kapta’s MESA architecture changes that equation with a modular, highly manufacturable approach to electronically steerable radar,” said Mina Faltas, Founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners. “We believe its combination of performance, cost, and scalability will make Kapta a foundational supplier to the next generation of U.S. and allied space architectures, and we’re thrilled to lead the Series A.”

articles.title: From H-1B to CEO: How Satya Nadella traveled the path the U.S. just cut off for Microsoft workers
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Satya Nadella arrived in the U.S. from India in 1988 to study computer science. Over the next three decades, he went from a temporary work visa to permanent residency to American citizenship, and rose up the ranks at Microsoft to become only the third CEO in its history.
“I don’t think my story would be possible anywhere else,” Nadella wrote in his 2017 book, “Hit Refresh.” “I am proud today to call myself an American citizen.”

On Thursday, President Trump personally handed the Microsoft CEO the National Medal of Technology and Innovation. The award cited his “transformative leadership of a critical American technology company, which led to its rejuvenation for a new era of cloud computing.”

Nadella thanked Trump on X , writing that he was “humbled to stand alongside so many giants of American innovation.” The other honorees were Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell, who also received the technology medal; and Elon Musk, Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and AMD CEO Lisa Su, who received the National Medal of Science.
Five of the six were born outside the country.

Hours earlier, the Trump administration had suspended Microsoft from the federal program it uses to help foreign workers take the same path to permanent residency. Vice President JD Vance said the company had abused the system by laying off American workers while hiring foreign workers, and called H-1B workers “foreign indentured servants.”
“Our message to Microsoft is you’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers,” Vance said at a White House news conference .

Two different programs: The suspension doesn’t stop Microsoft from hiring foreign workers on H-1B visas. Those are temporary work visas, typically granted for three years at a time and generally limited to six years, with some exceptions. They’re overseen by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

Amazon is the bigger user of H-1B visas. It received more than 19,000 approvals for H-1B petitions in fiscal 2025, about three times Microsoft’s total, according to an analysis of USCIS data by the National Foundation for American Policy. The totals include renewals and extensions, so they don’t represent individual workers.
The program to which Microsoft lost access comes later in the process.

Known as PERM , it’s run by the Labor Department and is usually the first step when a company sponsors an employee to stay in the U.S. permanently. The employer has to advertise the job and show that no qualified, available U.S. worker can fill it. Most applications are for people already working in the U.S. on H-1B visas.

Microsoft is the biggest user of PERM. The Labor Department ruled on 3,161 of its applications in the fiscal year that ended in September 2025, more than for any other employer in the country, according to a GeekWire analysis of the agency’s data . Microsoft also led in the first nine months of fiscal 2026, with 1,683 applications decided through June.

Amazon and Google filed thousands of PERM applications in 2022 and early 2023, then largely stopped. The Labor Department ruled on 39 applications from Amazon and its subsidiaries last fiscal year, including Whole Foods, Audible and Zappos, and three from Google.

The suspension could hit hardest for Microsoft employees already on H-1B visas. Many count on the company to start the permanent residency process in time to extend their visas past the usual six-year limit, and the Labor Department says it won’t process Microsoft’s pending applications either.

Some Microsoft employees on H-1B visas were surprised by the news and unsure whether it would affect them, The Seattle Times reported . The paper noted that the White House hasn’t provided evidence of fraud by Microsoft.

Microsoft’s response: In a statement posted Thursday , Microsoft pushed back on criticism of its hiring and said it looks forward to “providing the Administration with additional information.” The statement focused on H-1B visas and didn’t address the PERM suspension specifically.

The company said about 80% of the roughly 6,000 H-1B applications it filed last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of people who already work at Microsoft. “These were not to hire new people,” it said.
The rest were for new hires already living in the U.S. legally, a group equal to about 1% of Microsoft’s U.S. workforce. “They are not new arrivals to our country,” the company said.

Microsoft also said it files H-1B petitions only for workers who meet “the rigorous standards of this visa category,” pays them “the same as any other employees doing comparable work,” and offers wages “among the highest of all H-1B filings.”
The vast majority of its U.S. employees are Americans, the company said.

Nadella’s own path: Nadella’s route to citizenship wasn’t a straight line, as he described in “Hit Refresh.” He was working at Microsoft when he married his wife, Anu, in India in December 1992. The next summer, her application for a visa to join him in the U.S. was rejected because she was married to a permanent resident.
Spouses of permanent residents faced long waits, and Microsoft’s immigration lawyer told Nadella it could take five years or more to bring her to the U.S.

Nadella considered quitting Microsoft and moving back to India. Then the lawyer suggested a different approach: give up his permanent residency and go back to a temporary H-1B visa, which would let his wife join him right away.

In June 1994, Nadella went to the U.S. embassy in New Delhi, past the long lines of people hoping to get visas, and told a clerk he wanted to give up his permanent residency. The clerk was dumbfounded, Nadella wrote. The plan worked, and Anu joined him in Seattle, where they started a family. Nadella eventually got back on the path to permanent residency and later became a U.S. citizen.

But in the meantime, back in Redmond, Nadella became known around the Microsoft campus as the guy who gave up his green card. Colleagues called him for advice. One, Kunal Bahl, later left Microsoft when his H-1B ran out before his permanent residency came through. He returned to India and founded the e-commerce company Snapdeal.
“Such is the perverse logic of this immigration law,” Nadella wrote.

articles.title: Microsoft 2.5: GitHub COO Kyle Daigle on stitching the developer universe together
articles.author: Mary Jo Foley
paras: GeekWire is profiling over the next few weeks some of the people and teams that are shaping the evolution of Microsoft in what we’re calling its “Microsoft 2.5” era .

A delicate dance: In August 2025, Microsoft moved to integrate GitHub into the mothership, under its CoreAI division, after having allowed it to run as a quasi-independent entity since acquiring it in 2018. At the same time, GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke announced he would leave the company at the end of the year.

A number of developers feared the worst: GitHub would become just another arm of Microsoft and lose the community-mindedness that had made it attractive to developers of all stripes, and especially open-source ones.

GitHub Chief Operating Officer Kyle Daigle — a 13-plus-year GitHub veteran — had been one of the main champions of the need to “keep GitHub GitHub.” He maintained that stance even after he added the “Chief Marketing Officer of Developer” title for all of Microsoft to his COO role in January 2026.

So, how has Microsoft done this past year with managing GitHub? In an interview with GeekWire , Daigle acknowledged that GitHub’s relationship with Microsoft has changed since the end of the standalone CEO era. But the goal is no longer just “don’t break GitHub.” It’s to export GitHub’s community, developer-first ethos and learnings across Microsoft.

GitHub has influence beyond just the GitHub product set now, Daigle said. And the fact that Microsoft opted to consolidate its developer-facing messaging and community outreach under Daigle, someone who came from GitHub, not from Microsoft’s traditional DevDiv organization, gives weight to his claim.

“Bringing teams together — engineering teams and marketing teams and everyone that wasn’t talking to each other before — has been a really big part of the work,” Daigle said. “I see all these opportunities for GitHub to directly help and impact the overall mission of Microsoft versus keeping it cloistered in a way that isn’t helping either GitHub’s mission or Microsoft’s mission.”

These days, developer teams across Microsoft and GitHub are sharing foundations and the GitHub Copilot software development kit across organizations “in a way that would have seemed improbable before,” he said.
As Microsoft historians know, “Microsoft’s challenge isn’t creating products. It’s connecting them,” Daigle said.

Growing pains: At the same time, the rise of AI agents has strained GitHub’s infrastructure. Over the past few months, GitHub has experienced some significant outages, including one in August that lasted nearly eight hours .

GitHub officials have said they are migrating from their own datacenters to Azure to try to ease some of the capacity issues. Daigle said it’s not a simple lift-and-shift process; rather, it’s a major re-architecture for the platform.
GitHub is roughly 60% through its Azure migration as of early October, he said.

It’s working with Azure storage teams on separating compute and storage for the Git distributed version control system to help alleviate bottlenecks caused by developers and agents working concurrently in the same repositories. Developers and agents made 7.38 billion commits on GitHub in September alone, according to the company.

GitHub’s recent growth would not have been manageable without Microsoft scaling expertise and Azure support, Daigle said. GitHub is in a unique position of being able to request major additional capacity, such as millions of CPUs, and work with Microsoft teams to provision it, he said.

The GitHub app and agent store: GitHub got its start as a platform for source control and collaboration. But its role is evolving as part of its Microsoft integration. In addition to developing and supporting Microsoft’s most successful Copilot, GitHub Copilot, GitHub has an important place in Microsoft’s agent-centric strategy.

GitHub is becoming “the store for anything that needs to be coded and needs some verification,” Daigle said. “We’ll connect you to whatever the right tool inside of Microsoft is for you to run that or whatever tool you’re using, not just (from) the Microsoft product suite.”

In the new world order, GitHub isn’t just the store for apps. Increasingly, it’s also the store for agents, which means GitHub is acting as the developer layer for Microsoft’s “agent factory” strategy.

(Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates envisioned Microsoft as a “software factory” that could produce software at scale. These days, CEO Satya Nadella and team talk about Microsoft as an “ agent factory,” helping customers create agents at scale.)
GitHub currently serves more than 200 million developers, plus an unknown but quickly growing number of agents.

Developers need to be thinking in new ways when it comes to agents, Daigle said. They need to consider ideas such as scaling application programming interfaces (APIs) for agents separately from humans, creating APIs designed specifically for agents, rewriting documentation and tooling so agents can consume GitHub efficiently, and treating agent access as a fundamentally different workload from human access.

In the longer term, Daigle said he expects AI to make software economically viable for smaller audiences, such as a family, an individual or a single team. The app-store model may change substantially in the coming years, as people create highly specialized applications. GitHub could help like-minded users discover software for specific interests, such as a narrowly focused household or community use case.

GitHub historically has considered anyone who has seen or touched code to be part of the developer community. Daigle’s vision is for GitHub and Microsoft to let both professional developers and newer builders create and run software and agents without needing to manage token costs, uptime, monitoring or operational overhead.

GitHub will have more to say about its plans at the GitHub Universe conference in San Francisco, Oct. 28-29. The event won’t focus on code generation alone; it will include information on tools covering the full lifecycle, proactive security approaches and how to determine whether software is working well after deployment.

“We’re looking to solve the core parts of the platform, like Git, like Actions, in a way that I hope will make people excited and feel like they can absolutely trust GitHub for the next decade to come,” Daigle said.

articles.title: Tug-of-War Over New Transportation Funding Heats Up in Bellevue
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The Bellevue City Council is on the cusp of approving a pair of new funding sources to bolster transportation infrastructure later this fall, but the fight over what exactly those new dollars should fund is far from settled. The debate playing out now is set to decide which transportation projects the Eastside's largest city prioritizes over the next decade, as it prepares to accommodate significant housing growth around public transit.

This week city officials formally presented a set of scenarios that outlined how Bellevue would use projected revenue from a potential 0.1% increase in the city's sales tax rate as well as a $20 car tab fee, unlocked from a transportation benefit district that the city has been considering tapping into since 2023. The sales tax bump would be expected to generate around $100 million for transportation infrastructure over 10 years, with the car tab only bringing in $20 million over the same period.

Sustainable transportation advocates in Bellevue have been pushing for a major infusion of resources to help reduce deaths and serious injuries, and that push has been backed up by a bloc of councilmembers standing behind the idea of prioritizing safety investments. But many of Bellevue's business interests are pushing for more investments in "underperforming" intersections to make it easier to drive around the city.

If the Council decides to adopt both the sales tax hike and the car tab next month, Bellevue would be poised to invest an additional $35 million over a decade in bike and pedestrian improvement projects, as well as $16.4 million more in neighborhood traffic calming. Combined, those two categories would amount to 31% of the city's total transportation spending, a lower number than the 40% referenced by Transportation Director Andrew Singelakis this past spring during an initial budget discussion .

The "major projects" category would amount to a full 35% of spending, with the majority of those new dollars devoted to completing the next phase of Spring Boulevard (Zone 3) through the BelRed neighborhood. Framed as a multimodal project, the $74.8 million connection would create an alternative for pedestrian-hostile Bel-Red Road – which the Council decided against making safer for people on bikes in 2024 . But with two general purpose lanes beefing up the need for property acquisition, the benefits of the project for people who walk and bike in Bellevue won't really align with its cost.
There's also the fact that the road cuts right through what is intended to be a new park for the future residents of BelRed.

The scenarios laid out on Tuesday do invest plenty in vehicle capacity in their own right. Scenario two, which includes only the sales tax increase, includes $18.9 million in new funding for projects specifically intended to address driver travel times on top of $49.3 million under the status quo. That includes $10 million to widen two intersections to improve traffic flow. With scenario three, which includes the new car tab fee, that would increase to $25 million, getting another intersection widening across the finish line.

There's also the issue of the Grand Connection Crossing , Bellevue's plan to build a pedestrian bridge over I-405 between Downtown and Wilburton and create a brand new multimodal connection as well as an opportunity for placemaking. Under either scenario 2 or 3, the $265 million project would receive a $10 million investment, freeing up dollars that had been set to go to the crossing from the general fund – dollars that could potentially go to any other city spending. Recently the City of Bellevue received buy-in from several regional governments to tap into tax-increment financing to pay for a much bigger share of that project's total cost.

These potential funding sources recently won over a major Bellevue stakeholder. Three years ago, the Bellevue Chamber of Commerce had initially opposed the idea of tapping into the unutilized transportation benefit district, which cities like Seattle have long been using to fund infrastructure. But now they've come around, officially conveying support for the move Tuesday night. But the business group, which has convened a Bellevue Mobility Coalition to weigh in on transportation issues, has conditions.

The group has framed an intense desire to see the sales tax revenue generated by the 0.1% increase – "paid largely by businesses" – serve the city's high-growth areas like Downtown, Wilburton, Factoria, and Eastgate. The smaller tranche of car tab funding, the group said in an October 6 letter, should "primarily benefit neighborhoods."

In comments Tuesday night, a Chamber representative also told councilmembers they want to see any additional funding that comes in beyond projections get devoted to vehicle infrastructure – namely intersections that are considered "deficient" in terms of how much delay drivers experience getting through them. The group also made clear that they don't support the idea of repurposing traffic lanes to create bicycle facilities, one of the most cost-effective ways for cities to make streets safer.

"Our support depends on four things. First, funding for Spring Boulevard Zone 3, 120th Avenue NE Stage 4, and the Grand Connection stays sufficient to complete the projects," Tony Sprague, Public Policy Manager for the Bellevue Chamber of Commerce, told councilmembers. "Second, the underperforming intersections fund is increased and focused on growth corridor arterials with the first $10 million of any surplus sales tax collections dedicated. Third, vehicular capacity is not reduced for bicycle facilities except as a last resort. Fourth, sales tax revenue is not shifted to neighborhood programs that the car tab should fund."

Mariya Frost, Vice President of Government Affairs for Kemper Development Company (a member of the Bellevue Mobility Coalition), went even further than the Chamber, requesting that the Council put the revenue sources to a public vote and suggesting the proposals invest too much in walking and biking. The company, which recently announced an intention to sell its holdings in Bellevue, has been actively involved in transportation decisions in the city going back decades.

"If council decides to move forward without a public vote, project funding must prioritize traffic congestion relief and accommodating vehicular travel associated with Bellevue's growth," Frost said. "The rationale I've heard is that we need to balance the system across all modes, but it makes little sense to disproportionately pour millions of dollars into lower demand infrastructure while the roadway network carrying nearly 70% of our workers and residents is actively breaking down."
But so far Councilmember Jared Nieuwenhuis has been the lone voice on council framing either scenario as investing too much in walking and biking.

"Throughout the different scenarios, there's substantially more funding for bikes and pedestrians than vehicles," Nieuwenhuis said. "You're looking for that balanced approach, [a] multimodal approach. I totally agree with that, but I'm also cognizant of the fact the vast majority of people that who come into our city do so in a vehicle, in their car."

Other councilmembers have only expressed frustration that the investments the city has planned aren't able to be implemented sooner, but also haven't signaled a willingness to rebalance any of the funding scenarios by prioritizing safety projects over intersection widenings.

"Every year at this time, we have the Walk and Roll to School Day commitment proclamation. And I always think to myself, is it really safe to expect that our families are going to ask their kids to walk or roll to school?," Councilmember Lynne Robinson said. "And I know every year it gets a little safer, but we have so many holes in our infrastructure that most families I don't think do feel comfortable having their kids get to school independently, and that just creates a huge line of cars and congestion in our neighborhoods."
Councilmember Naren Briar made similar remarks, echoing comments she made back in April about wanting to see more funding devoted to neighborhood traffic calming and safety upgrades.

"If a seven-year-old has no sidewalks or a crosswalk to rely on when waiting for the bus in the dark at 7am, those children are our top concern for me, and their safety and their well-being, as opposed to prioritizing one mode over the other," Briar said. "I think neighborhood improvement is what I would really like to see. I understand that if we get to a place where taxes have to be raised, I do firmly believe that it needs to prevail through the scenario that benefits the neighborhoods the most."

While the attempt to strike a "balanced approach" illustrates Bellevue's current state as formerly car-oriented suburb trying to find a path toward being a more cosmopolitan place, there are signs that the reality of trying to keep planning around cars is starting to sink in.

"As we grow over the next 20 years, there will be limited capacity for additional vehicle facilities," Deputy Transportation Director Mark Poch said. "Right of way is limited. We have really good regional transportation we need to connect to, a lot of people connect to that by foot or by bike, as you know. Trying to find that balance so that we're able to meet that growth is really the key objective and making sure that we were aligned with what the community thinks – not one for one, but in the same ballpark, I think was important."
Bellevue's budget deliberations are set to continue throughout this month, with major decisions coming at November 3 and 10 meetings ahead of a final vote on November 17.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Fall Foliage
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: The leaves are finally starting to fall and there is no better place to admire King County’s incredible scenery than from a historic Metro bus. The annual Metro Employees Historic Vehicle Association (MEHVA) Fall Foliage Tour is back this year on October 25. Ride on one of the historic buses in MEHVA’s fleet through the Cascade foothills. Buses depart from 6th Ave S & S Royal Brougham Way (one block from Stadium station) at 11am and will return around 3pm. Tickets cost $10 and the group will stop for lunch along the way.

If you prefer to stay in Seattle, the Washington Park Arboretum is incredible this time of year. The arboretum is located just west of Madison Park, near stops for routes 8, 11, 43, 48, and the G Line. UW station is the closest Link station, about a 20 minute walk from the park.

articles.title: At Capitol Hill Station, Cha Chak changes the balance on Thai tea
articles.author: AGPhoto
paras: $5 A MONTH TO HELP KEEP CHS PAYWALL-FREE Subscribe to CHS to help hire writers and photographers to cover the neighborhood. CHS is a pay what you can community news site with no required sign-in or paywall. To stay that way, we need you. Become a subscriber to help us cover the neighborhood for $5 a month -- or choose your level of support Behind the Cha Chak counter above Capitol Hill Station , making tea looks a lot like pulling espresso.

Servers pour hot tea back and forth between two metal pitchers held wide apart, repeating the motion until the liquid turns frothy and smooth. It is cha chak, the hand-pulled tea style common in southern Thailand and Malaysia. Owner Montida Lertkiatsakul compares the process to steaming milk for a latte. It is not about the dairy, she explains, but about working air into the liquid to create texture.
That aeration carries a brew designed to taste fundamentally different from syrupy takeout versions.
“Usually the Thai iced tea tends to have a lot of milk taste,” Lertkiatsakul said.

Cha Chak blends several strong black teas to keep the flavor bold and significantly less sweet, finishing with a slight bitterness. The green tea skips matcha powder for a green tea base scented with jasmine. Coconut milk is available as a dairy alternative, along with caffeine-free options.

The shop sits on the plaza across from Glo’s Diner , taking over the space left empty where a chain juice bar closed in 2024. It is Lertkiatsakul’s second business on the Hill, coming a decade after she helped opened Manao Thai Street Eats at 14th and Pine. She partnered with Suphanita Roumsak on the new project.
“It’s a good location and a good community,” Lertkiatsakul said.

Desserts share the menu with the tea. Cha Chak serves Thai tea chiffon cake, green tea ice cream lattes, and scoops of mango, chai, and green tea ice cream. A mango sticky rice sundae is also on offer, made with a house mango sauce during the months outside the brief spring window when fresh Thai mangoes are in season.

For visitors, the draw is a rare look at traditional Southeast Asian tea mechanics paired with a menu built from scratch. Between the live theater of hand-pulled brewing, an intentionally bold, less-sugary tea profile, and house-made sweets like the mango sticky rice sundaes and tea chiffon cakes, Cha Chak gives the station plaza a distinct craft alternative.
Find Cha Chak at 118 Broadway E above the plaza along E Barbara Bailey Way. Learn more at chachakseattle.com .

articles.title: 15th Ave E is joining the Hilloween trick or treat hot zone — Plus, pictures from the annual Volunteer Park Halloween Pet Parade
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: More pictures from last year in the trick or treat hot zone here

The merchants of 15th Ave E are also scaring up lots of Hilloween spirit this year. The neighborhood’s businesses have announced they will host a special 15th Ave E extension of the area’s annual trick or treating hot zone in the streets of North Capitol Hill near Volunteer Park .

15th Ave E’s restaurants, shops, and businesses are working together for a night of trick or treating on Saturday, October 31st starting at 4 PM. The plan is to have candy for trick-or-treaters with free jack-o-lantern buckets and maps at participating businesses. You can find the roster of participating businesses and more details here .
Just a short walk from the popular Capitol Hill trick or treating areas around 16th Ave E and 17th Ave E, the 15th Ave E celebration will be part of day of expanded Hilloween fun in 2026.
CHS reported here on the revival of the annual Hilloween carnival and trick or treating across Broadway and Pike/Pine also taking place this year.
Enterprising candy collectors can plan a route that starts in Pike/Pine early in the day, winds through Broadway, and then up to 15th before topping off their buckets in the trick or treat hot zone .
The Halloween Pet Parade organized by the Volunteer Park Trust has already kicked off the season on Capitol Hill. Here are some pictures from this year’s parade. Happy Hilloween!

articles.title: Welcome to The Stranger’s October 2026 Issue
articles.author: Vivian McCall
paras: After giving years of my life to this paper and reaching the point of my career where people have to listen to me, I’m returning to the marsh I crawled out of, Chicago. Have I lost my mind?

I’m writing to you from the road. In the last 30 hours, I have bruised my entire body hauling my most prized possessions down the stairs, gifted my less-than-prized possessions to a curb in Capitol Hill, woke up in a state where it is illegal for me to pee, and spent exorbitantly on gas thanks to Trump’s idiot war in Iran. I am on US Route 212 East, where I am on deer watch. Deer undermine what should be our shared mission of keeping them alive by running stupidly at death. Oh, another dead one. Congrats to her; this was her Jellicle Ball.

I am not insane. I am moving home for a job at our sister publication, the Chicago Reader . The box merchant at UPS did not agree that moving to Chicago is sane. He thought all the neighborhoods were very scary. Incorrect. Only some of them are very scary, like River North. It sucks there. Part of moving back is trading tech bros for just bros. I can accept this. My coworkers cannot accept this, and I take their displeasure as a sign of unyielding love and admiration. Don’t be embarrassed. It’s mutual.

I spent five years and two months of my life in Seattle, three years and five months of them at The Stranger . It defined my life here, mostly because working at The Stranger leaves a person with very little extra time. All the near deer strikes have given me the space to consider two things: which of my prized possessions would embed itself in my skull if we crashed into a deer right now, and what it means to be a Stranger writer.

I only have 400 words, so I’ll keep this brief, using examples from this very issue: Stranger writers must be funny (pg. 24), hungry and/or thirsty (pg. 47), emotionally intelligent (pg. 35), emotionally unintelligent (pg. 8), aware of what makes this city special (pg. 43), and sick of what makes this city fucking suck sometimes (pg. 12). Lastly, a Stranger writer often works when they aren’t supposed to, like when they’re the designated deer spotter at 10 p.m. on a cross-country road trip.

Perhaps this is all too much crawling into my own ass. In my defense, it is very warm, and Chicago is very cold. I am finishing this in South Dakota, where the only gender is biker. My girlfriend is setting up our new electric account. Wall Drug awaits. I wrote 48 words over.
Sacrificing a hot dog pin to the Bikini Kill mosh pit
Wearing a dress covered in sequins and spinning around and around and around in it until you almost fall over at the Genius Awards in front of everyone you know
Not All Men™ but certainly most of them at this point!
Spilling a whole sample of Troye Sivan’s perfume on myself
OTTOGI Otoki Cheesy Ramen made with frozen peas and the cheese powder packet’s “cheese pro” level
Tongue kissing your dog after he ate peanuts
Prophesizing a car crash, and then becoming a car crash victim

articles.title: Scarecrow Video’s 2026 Psychotronic Challenge: Week Two
articles.author: Audrey Vann and Julianne Bell
paras: Welcome to October! It’s the most wonderful time of the year, when I mitigate my seasonal depression by going all in on gothic literature and horror films. The good people at the world’s best video store, Scarecrow Video, have put together their 2026 Psychotronic Challenge , which contains 31 prompts for a movie each day throughout the month.
The rules are simple: watch at least one film each day that falls under the psychotronic category “in whatever order suits you,” and “have fun and get weird.”

Scarecrow defines “psychotronic” as “denoting or relating to a genre of films that typically have a science fiction, horror, or fantasy theme and were made on a low budget.” But the staff also notes that they don’t necessarily subscribe to the “low budget” definition in order to allow more diversity in the selection. “That being said,” they write, “we do like an underdog more often than not” so “you might as well have a lot of fun pushing yourself to new lows.”

My colleague Audrey Vann and I compiled a list of our picks for the second week, which includes our favorite genres: creepy dolls, homoeroticism, and witches who worship Marilyn Monroe. Stay tuned for weekly posts with suggestions throughout the month, and catch up on week one if you haven’t already. Support your local video store, and happy viewing! –Julianne Bell

Watch Bride of Chucky for an amazing soundtrack (Blondie, Judas Priest, Slayer, Billy Idol) and an even more amazing makeover scene .
More ideas: Shocker (1989), Frankenhooker (1990), Pet Sematary 2 (1992), Re-Animator (1985), Blackenstein (1973)
9. SHOWER POWER: Bathe your eyeballs in a shocking shower scene.

Last fall I saw Basket Case director Frank Henenlotter’s 1988 horror comedy Brain Damage for the first time, and I would recommend going in as blind as possible. Keep your eyes peeled for a steamy homoerotic shower scene starring beefcake bodybuilder Joe Gonzalez, who also appears as a pimp in our upcoming Day 17 pick, Frankenhooker (also directed by Henenlotter).
More ideas: Psycho (1960), The Evil Dead (1981), Carrie (1976), Nightmare on Elm Street 5 (1989) , Arachnophobia (1990)
10. HOWLOWEEN: Dig up a flick with some canine inclusion, bones and all. Now who wants a belly rub?

I am utterly in love with the 2000 Canadian cult classic Ginger Snaps . In a sleepy Ontario suburb, misfit teen sisters Brigitte (Emily Perkins) and Ginger (Katherine Isabelle) have a pact to either move out or kill themselves together by age 16. When Ginger is bitten by a werewolf, choas and violence ensue. Many people have noted the film’s themes of feminism and female puberty, but I recommend you also check out Letterboxd user Sally Jane Black’s trans analysis . By the way, Brigitte and Ginger would make a killer Halloween costume duo if you’re looking for ideas! More ideas: Cujo (1983), The Company of Wolves (1984), Dracula’s Dog (1977), Frankenweenie (1984)
11. AT THE MAUL: There will be some slashin’ at the center of fashion, whether it’s prices, throats or big winter coats.

I’m obsessed with malls, so I was always going to love the Diablo Cody-produced comedy horror film Forbidden Fruits . Director Meredith Alloway co-wrote the screenplay with playwright Lily Houghton, based on Houghton’s 2019 stage play Of the woman came the beginning of sin, and through her we all die . The film follows a clique of three fruit-named cool-girl employees of a Free People-esque store who rule the mall: queen bee Apple (Lili Reinhart), bimbo Cherry (the inimitable Victoria Pedretti), and brainy Fig (Alexandra Shipp). New girl Pumpkin (Lola Tung) is initiated into the girlboss crew and learns that they’re actually a feminist coven of witches who worship Marilyn Monroe and stage occult rituals in the mall basement. It’s the perfect combo of The Craft , Jennifer’s Body , and Mean Girls —my only complaints are that the dialogue falls a bit flat at times and it should’ve been much gayer, but I’ll let it slide. More ideas: Chopping Mall (1986) Buffy the Vampire Slayer (1992), Night of the Comet (1984), Phantom of the Mall: Eric’s Revenge (1989), Dawn of the Dead (1978)
12. BACK IN THE SATELLITE: Rope yourself into a space western.

Nude on the Moon is Doris Wishman’s second of eight (!) nudist films that she co-directed and produced in the early 1960s. The premise is simple: a man inherits a ton of money and decides to invest in the development of a rocket (many such cases, unfortunately). Once he and his mentor land on the moon, they discover a civilization of topless women who worship at the foot of the Moon Queen (another topless woman, but she has her own throne).
More ideas: Galexina (1980), The Phantom Empire (1935), Barbarella (1968)
13. THIS IS A TINY TOWN: The sheriff would prefer you left before “something bad” happens.
Julianne’s pick: Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma (2026)

I Saw the TV Glow director Jane Schoenbrun’s latest film, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma , contains all my favorite things: queer horror, summer camp, psychosexual obsession, a sultry sapphic age-gap pairing, snacks, dipping sauces, X-Files icon Gillian Anderson, and Hacks actress Hannah Einbinder. As the credits rolled, I just sat there in silence thinking, “Well, this is it for me. I’ll probably never see a movie this catered to my specific interests ever again.” Einbinder stars as Kris, an up-and-coming queer filmmaker who is enlisted to direct a reboot of the slasher series Camp Miasma . She becomes fixated on casting the reclusive Billy Presley (Anderson), who played the franchise’s original final girl back in the day and now lives on the abandoned sleepaway camp set with her own private theater. The movie evokes the cozy-scary vibes of a small-town slasher, complete with convenience store cashiers who ask things like, “Where is it that you kids think you’re going?” Frankly, I want to live there!
More ideas: The Birds (1963), Cherry Falls (2000), House of Wax (2005), S tepford Wives (1975), Disturbing Behavior (1998)
14. SUBJECT TO SURVEILLABILITY: Ever feel like you’re being watched?

I saw Satoshi Kon’s anime psychological thriller Perfect Blue at SIFF on Audrey’s recommendation two years ago, and it is easily one of the most disturbing and terrifying films I have ever seen in my life. The movie revolves around Mima, a member of a J-pop girl group who leaves to become a full-time actress. However, this career move upsets her fanbase, and as a mysterious stalker begins targeting her, she begins to lose her grip on reality. Darren Aronofsky licensed the rights for this film to recreate a bathtub scene in Requiem for a Dream and clearly took more than a little inspiration from it for Black Swan , although he denies the latter—I’ll direct you to this shot-for-shot comparison and let you be the judge. (Major content warning for depiction of sexual assault—Mima films a graphic rape scene for a movie role, so please take care of yourself and choose one of our alternative picks if this one isn’t right for you.)
More ideas: Peeping Tom (1960), Body Double (1984), Blue Velvet (1986), The Watcher in the Attic (1976), Private Parts (1972)

articles.author: Stranger Election Control Board
paras: Don’t want to read? Skip to our Cheat Sheet !
It’s that time of year again, time for a cabal of vulgar Marxists in a hot conference room on Capitol Hill to handpick the government. Just kidding. We fixed the AC in the conference room.

Why go through the trouble of voting? A city council seat in District 5 could undermine the moderate majority in what we predict will be their last year on the dais, the State Supreme Court is up for grabs, and the futures of tax reform and trans kids are on the ballot.

Washington has the second most unequal tax structure of any state due to an insane State Supreme Court ruling from the Great Depression that makes taxing rich people’s income more than poor people’s illegal. Progressive legislators got organized enough to pass the Millionaires Tax as a test case to hopefully overturn that ruling, which is why the right has backed conservative candidates in the five races for State Supreme Court, and dumped millions into a ballot initiative to repeal this potentially transformative legislation. The other two initiatives are anti-trans and antigay nonsense, so you should vote against all three.

There’s also a possibility of flipping a few Republican state legislative seats this year, though not so much in deep-blue Greater Seattle, where it’s more important to replace moderate Democrats with progressives who aren’t afraid to tax the rich. (Read our full endorsements at TheStranger.com.)

Based on our desire to support candidates who are actually capable of delivering progressive policy wins, the SECB took some flak in the primary for not endorsing two candidates Seattle’s mayor did, because apparently some people think we work for her (she would return our calls if we did). Upper management also coincidentally decided to let our editor-in-chief go right before we published primary endorsements, fanning the flames spread by rumormongers and spurned candidates that the paper’s owners interfered with endorsements. We heard many fanciful rumors about our bosses stopping the presses to replace our opinions with theirs. But that didn’t happen. We’ve also heard that the board has been stuffed with allegiants at the beck and call of our investors. As if. Our staff has a clause in our union contract to prevent interference in endorsements, and allowing the business side of the paper to interfere with editorial direction is a big ethical no-no in our profession that would’ve led several of us to resign in protest.

As we’ve explained ad nauseam by now, the SECB endorsed incumbent Senate Majority Leader Jamie Pedersen over first-time candidate Hannah Sabio-Howell because he’s quarterbacking the once-in-a-generation income tax reform fight and replacing him would also mean a more conservative Senate caucus. Washington’s conservatives think so, too, which is why they’ve spent tens of thousands of dollars opposing Pedersen’s reelection, and the whole race has become a referendum on progressive tax reform, whether you like it or not. Regardless of our actual logic, the SECB got tarred as compromised by corporate interests for this (no, we don’t get the logic either) as well as for not endorsing YIMBY tech bro Ron Davis, who didn’t have a backup plan for fumbling his interview with us. A tip for candidates seeking political office: If you’re going to spend thousands of dollars on yard signs, make sure they say “vote for me” instead of advertising that you lost The Stranger’s endorsement. Your donors will thank you.

Though the SECB is leftist, progressive, and kind of annoying, we are not yes-men for any candidate who occupies the leftmost lane. Our political class knows they have to appeal to the community’s progressive majority whether they share their beliefs or not, and you would not believe the number of moderates who walk through our doors hoping we will launder their reactionary politics to our readers. Think of us as six overworked food safety inspectors at a slaughterhouse trying to let as little contaminated meat out the door as possible. And folks, there is poop on a lot of this meat .

Our health code is journalistic scrutiny: We scour their voting records and financial reports. We call their current and former associates. We compile hefty research documents for our colleagues. We conduct panel interviews so they can tell us exactly how they plan to execute progressive policy, and then we discuss at length whom each of us would endorse. We frequently disagree, delay votes to hunt down key facts, and take vote after vote until we reach a simple majority. Then we write an endorsement and bicker some more. The only people who see it before it’s published are the SECB, a copy editor, and a fact-checker. Our bosses and colleagues often find out who we endorse the day we go to press.

We joke that we handpick candidates, but The Stranger is not a political machine. We are not interested in performing politics or propaganda. We are an independent newspaper that informs our progressive readers which candidates most align with their political goals.

You’ll find explanations behind each endorsement in this paper and online. You can see similar decisions spanning decades on our website. Sometimes people are happy with us, sometimes they are very angry. That’s politics.

If this doesn’t sit right with you, and you think we should be using our influence to be a rubber stamp, to be good soldiers for the progressive movement, then congratulations, you don’t want fucking journalism. You want friends and associates of politicians to tell you how to vote. Don’t like how much power we exert in primary elections? Then you’d better get organized! The business community sure is.

The SECB does not endorse in uncontested races, races we forgot, or races in Spokane. Its members include, for a second time, Vivian McCall, Megan Seling, Charles Mudede, Nathalie Graham, Hunter Pauli, Cedar Attanasio, and Gracie, the privately owned Texas giraffe.
Vote (Fuck) No on I-001, I-638, and I-645

Brian Heywood and his outfit, Let’s Go Washington, are the stupidest, most destructive motherfuckers in the state of Washington. These know-nothings push culturally conservative ballot initiatives as a front for their real aim: convincing people much poorer than them to defend their wealth and prevent their millionaire money from being used for the benefit of society.

Vote no on all three of these Let’s Go Washington initiatives, all of which are so silly and counterproductive that even the conservative bozos on the Seattle Times Editorial Board saw them as low-effort, self-serving trash.

I-001 is an attempt to resurrect the Parents’ Bill of Rights (PBOR), which is not about parents or rights. It is about control and keeping students from seeking the support of trusted adults. It gave parents essentially no new rights. But inside this harmless, sensible exterior was a bomb. Ripped directly from a 2014 Louisiana law, the PBOR could’ve handed private counseling records, detailing the private feelings, sexualities, and struggles of children, to their overbearing or unsupportive parents. It also could’ve buried school districts in onerous exemption paperwork. After the PBOR earned enough signatures to end up on the ballot in 2024, it was proactively adopted by the Legislature so it could be dismantled. If it passed, they wouldn’t have been able to touch it. Slapping a law made for one state onto the established legal code of another is fucking stupid and created numerous conflicts the Legislature later resolved and amended. The folks at Let’s Go Washington couldn’t handle that, so they’ve made it our problem again. Vote No.

If passed, I-638 would be the most extreme trans sports ban in the country, mandating genital exams, genetic testing, and hormonal testing for girls playing sports in high school, middle school, and in some cases, elementary school. Trans people have never dominated sports and there is zero evidence they ever will dominate sports. But requiring this shit is a great way to get a child molested, exclude a girl with high testosterone from competing, and create a higher barrier to entry for every girl who wants to play a school sport, all to keep somewhere between 10 and 20 trans people off the fields and courts. No, no, no.

The big kahuna, the real reason for the season, is I-645, an initiative to repeal the Millionaires Tax. Unless you’ve been living under a rock, you’ve heard that the Millionaires Tax, a 9.9 percent tax on all income above $1 million, is the first chess move toward a checkmate, graduated income tax in Washington State. It’s also sorely needed revenue for essential government services, public school, statewide universal free school lunches, health care and behavioral health care services, and human services. Contrary to popular speculation, it’s not going to chase every rich person out of the state. To make this real simple: If you’re not a millionaire, vote no on I-645. If you’re a millionaire, be a pal and vote no on I-645. We thank you for your service and for your continued residency in this state. We know a fair tax is not enough to drive you from our moderate climate and rugged, emerald vistas.

We all have a civic duty to stop taking this charlatan Brian Heywood seriously, or at least stop casting him as a political maverick unafraid of speaking hard truths. He is a dragon nestled on his golden horde, a rich and powerful man with the cash to amplify his voice over the thousands he seeks to politically and monetarily disempower. Vote no on these initiatives and pierce Heywood’s dragon heart.
Vote Yes on Prop 1 to Approve the Seattle Transit Measure

Hey, do you like the bus? Do you like when your bus is on time? What about when your bus still runs on the weekends or—gasp—after 10 p.m.? Well, then you’re really going to like the Seattle Transit Measure. We’ve had this citywide levy since 2014. We typically renew it every six years. This year’s renewal is the biggest ever. Proposed by Mayor Katie Wilson and passed by the Seattle City Council, it adds a sales tax increase of 0.15 percent, bringing the total sales tax to fund transit service to 0.3 percent, and it’ll last for 10 years this time. That’s huge, but voters need to approve it. Not only will it sustain current bus service, but it will add 100,000 extra service hours in the city. Plus, it includes maintenance dollars for transportation improvements. If we’re lucky, some of that money will add late-night buses, so you’re not stranded in the dark after a long night of grinding on your leather daddy at Massive. Everybody wins! And if this doesn’t pass, bus service is fucked. So there’s no alternative. Vote Yes.
United States Representative Congressional District 1 Suzan DelBene

Like many right-leaning corporate Democrats, Suzan DelBene lives in a castle made of money. Its walls, ramparts, drawbridges, and boiling pots of oil protect her from barbarian challengers on the left and the right, while she tosses enough cake from the portcullis to stave off the seizure of her ho-hum dominion by a people-powered political uprising.

What truly distinguishes DelBene is independent wealth. Far from a pedestrian millionaire, she jumped into tech early, and is sitting on upwards of $120 million. She is the richest congressperson in Washington State. Any person living a life like hers exists in a reality-distorting, super-dense black hole of privilege. So excuse us for disbelieving her promise to fix an unequal tax system she benefits from. Hating RFK Jr., loving abortion, and fighting a cartoonishly evil AI that denies care to seniors is not enough. In an interview with the SECB this summer, DelBene was allergic to specifics such as: name one tax loophole closed by you and your colleagues.

Expect the bare minimum from DelBene and accept there isn’t anyone else to put our faith in at the moment. The platform of her Republican opponent, Mary Silva, has more dog whistles than Westminster. Medical “freedom,” “secure” elections, parental “rights” in health care, it’s all there. However, we agree with Silva on at least two points: that dismantling mass surveillance is of critical concern for democracy, and that Henry Kissinger was a real bastard.
Until our country limits money in politics, we’ll be voting for its living, breathing consequences. Vote DelBene.
United States Representative Congressional District 7 Pramila Jayapal

Pramila Jayapal is one of the least compromising people in the miserable, undrained mire that is the US Congress. Jayapal, who led the Congressional Progressive Caucus for six years, can say what other Democrats will not: that Israel is committing a genocide, a stance she has backed up by pushing to end arms exports to the country and signing onto a congressional letter asking the State Department to investigate Israel’s illegal nuclear weapons arsenal. That not a cent of our tax dollars should go to ICE, and that DHS, a post-9/11 chimera from the War on Terror, should not even exist. That Democrats need to gerrymander congressional districts until we pass the John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act. That former Seattle Mayors Jenny Durkan and Ed Murray totally suck. (Mayor Katie Wilson? Well, she’s “getting her footing.”) And the Iran war? She says fuck the Iran war—in spirit, if not in those exact words—because it has “no clear mission, no strategy, no end goal.”

Jayapal sponsored “Housing Not Handcuffs,” a bill to limit the euphemistic “camping bans” that criminalize homeless people for sleeping outside, and the Trans Bill of Rights to protect gender-nonconforming people from discrimination in health care, housing, education, and public accommodations. Every time you drive over the West Seattle Bridge, remember that Jayapal helped secure the funds for its repair.
Jayapal wouldn’t bite when we asked if her coworker Congressman Hakeem Jeffries should lead the party. But as Hakeem Jeffries reminds us every day, nobody is perfect.

Even Nirav Sheth, the retired Lakewood policeman and former intelligence liaison for Customs and Border Patrol who insisted he was not a Republican even though he is running as one, said at our endorsement meeting this summer that meeting her was an honor. He wore an almost reverent expression at times. Vote Jayapal.
United States Representative Congressional District 8 Kim Schrier
Say you’re stranded on a desert island. Do you drink hot piss, or drink seawater and die? If you want to survive, it is bottoms up for piss, and for voting Kim Schrier.

With Republicans taking advantage of the gutted Voting Rights Act by redistricting their states David Duke–edly, Democrats will need every vote they can get to #resist this administration until 2028, when they (maybe) take over and resume fumbling the bag.

Not that we can count on Schrier to vote with most Democrats, or even vote against evil things. She voted for the Laken Riley Act, which allows ICE to detain undocumented immigrants accused of theft indefinitely, and other dumb shit, like a bill to sanction the International Criminal Court for going after Israel for its war crimes, a bill allowing the US Attorney General to publish a list of local and state entities that offer cashless bail, a resolution condemning the “horrors” of socialism in “all its forms,” and taking seemingly every opportunity to strip DC’s control of its criminal justice system. She was also one of 21 Democrats who voted to end the government shutdown on February 3, just 10 days after Alex Pretti was shot dead in Minneapolis, when the party had a modicum of leverage. Hnnnnnggggg.
Her opponent, Republican Trinh Ha, is somehow worse. Her solidly conservative platform includes “strong schools,” “smart immigration,” a “people-first economy,” and “learn more.” No thank you.

At least Schrier is for universal pre-K, and for codifying DACA and the DREAM Act, and she definitely believes in human-caused climate change. Our hands are tied, but our mouths are wide open. Drink the piss. Vote Schrier.
United States Representative Congressional District 9 Adam Smith
The only reason we can present as to why you should vote for Adam Smith is that a Democratic majority in Congress could gum up some of the works of Trump 2. That’s it. We have zero other reasons.

articles.title: King County Holds Heartbreakingly Vast Funeral for People With Nobody to Bury Them
articles.author: Sarah Anne Lloyd
paras: There are 626 people, the most King County has ever interred at one time through its indigent remains program , stacked neatly beneath a fresh marble grave marker, each with cremains in their own plastic urn within a weathertight concrete crypt. It’s also the biggest jump the county has seen from a previous ceremony to the next; the last one, held in June 2025, honored 405. The ceremonies are not annual—they occur whenever there are enough remains to bury.

The crowd gathered at Mt. Olivet Cemetery in Renton on Wednesday is a typically Seattle mixed bag, with some in more formal black outfits and others in hoodies and jeans. Bagpipes—like most of the ceremony, performed by an enthusiastic volunteer—make the ceremony incredibly easy to find.

“The piper, he’s always wanted to be piping here at this ceremony,” says Joel Ingebritson, lead chaplain for the Seattle Fire Department and the King County Sheriff’s Office. “Everybody who’s here wants to be here to share this moment.”

There’s no one particular demographic that makes up the majority of the people laid to rest in these ceremonies. Many lived long lives—so long, in fact, that they outlived anyone who could have claimed their bodies. Some are infants who entered the world in challenging and traumatizing circumstances. Others had families or friends to claim them, but nobody who could afford a burial. Around 12 percent were experiencing homelessness at their time of death, ballparks James Sosik, Lead Forensic Medicolegal Investigator for King County Medical Examiner’s Office, between the years 2020 and 2025. (Demographic data for this year isn’t available yet.)

Some attendees are mourning a specific person among the 626, but more are here in reverence, to hold some space, however small, for each life on the list. Lori and Yolanda Rodriguez, sisters who work at an adult family home, came to pay their respects to a former resident who they call Esteban.

“He was just a very nice guy, you know,” says Yolanda, showing me a video of a lanky, elderly man with an infectious smile and a birthday cake. “After he came to us, he was kind of part of our family, you know? He had no family. So when he came to us, that’s how he felt.”

Clergy from multiple faiths take turns reading the names of the dead in 15 shifts, offering religious blessings in between—the ceremony is multi-faith, not faith-neutral. Some read from texts, while others offer prayers. A Buddhist leader sounds a chime alongside a blessing.

It takes three people just to get through the Bs. During the Js, someone tries to get a drone video, and the drone itself, rising up behind the silent, solemn crowd, sounds like a swarm of wasps. The reader persists.

After the final name, someone plays a brief farewell song on an acoustic guitar. Around half the attendees leave, but the rest linger, sitting with the enormity of the loss. Several leave bouquets on the marker.

The state paid for both the burial and funeral for people who died on public assistance until 1993, when the Legislature cut that funding. Washington’s counties scrambled to figure out how they could foot the bill respectfully.

King County implemented its program by the end of that year, and opted to only pay for cremations, and a communal burial for them, as a last resort. So it became the work of the Medical Examiner’s Office to start tracking down families—and often, when they find them, helping them find cremation or burial options that they can afford.

“But if some people just flat out say, ‘Man, I got nothing. I’m not working. My husband’s disabled. We’re on SSI. We just don’t have anything,’ I’m not gonna bust people’s balls about that,” clarifies Sosik. “I don’t wanna make them feel worse.”

Assistance finding an affordable burial starts early; Ingebritson tells me that when first responders respond to a death in the home, they “help them guide them to places where they can find a more affordable funeral.”

Still, after all that, 626 people had no other option but county cremation and burial. Without current demographic data, it’s hard to attribute the jump to any specific cause. Even Ingebritson and Sosik can only offer theories, although both bring up fentanyl; while overdose deaths have been on the decline since 2023, they remain significantly higher than they were five years ago.

Among the people here to pay their respects are three staffers from the People’s Memorial Association, which maintains a funeral assistance fund. I ask if they’ve seen an increase in requests for assistance amid skyrocketing final expenses.
“Absolutely,” responds Communications and Events Director Rachel LeBlanc, but since the fund is only donor-powered, “we’re really only able to help a couple of families a month.”
“What I’m thinking about is how many of those names are people who called me,” Administrative assistant Haley Costa says, “then I gave them the price and they didn’t call back.”

But there are always going to be those who don’t have anyone to contact—or nobody willing to claim them. Sometimes Sosik makes calls to next-of-kin letting them know about an unclaimed body with only cursing on the other line.
“It’s kind of upsetting when you’re caring more about this person that you don’t know than the people that do know,” he tells me.
The Rodriguez sisters tell me this won’t be the last ceremony they attend.
“And we have other [residents] that… don’t have family either,” says Yolanda. “So I mean, it’s gonna be the same place, the same thing, they’re gonna come here.”

articles.title: This Hurricane Should NEVER Have Happened… So How Did It?
articles.author: Cascade PBS Staff
paras: For some reason, hurricanes are terrified of South America. As long as we’ve been keeping track, it’s only EVER been hit by ONE! Hurricane Catarina was the hurricane that never should have happened. So how did it? We’ll take a tour of hurricane regions around the world to answer that question. And we’ll find out what Catarina can teach us about how hurricanes really work, and how they’re changing.

articles.title: How do human beings explain taking part in genocide? NAZA provides a chilling look | Omer Bartov
articles.author: Omer Bartov
paras: It’s easier to blame brutes and sadists for extreme violence. But as we see in the documentary, modern genocides are fueled by people who are uncomfortably recognizable

Werner Best, a senior SS official and jurist who helped organize the Nazi death squads that murdered hundreds of thousands of Jews, is also known for his statement: “We must destroy the enemy without hating him.” He belonged to a younger generation of Nazi technocrats, who despised the foul-mouthed, beer-bellied, brown-shirted “old fighters” of the Nazi party in the 1920s, and believed in organizing genocide neatly and dispassionately. After the fall of the regime, Best escaped justice for the rest of his long life, dying peacefully in Germany in 1989. His chilling statement came to my mind while I was watching the film NAZA.

I grew up in Tel Aviv and have visited there often in recent years. That is why the interviews with 24 Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers, which make up this documentary, felt strangely familiar. The conversations are conducted at night on rooftops, and the camera scans the cityscape, lingering on apartment windows as their inhabitants watch TV and make dinner. The landscape was intimately recognizable, and I felt a natural affinity with those people living their lives. I also recognized the way the interviewees talked – their speech patterns and choice of words. They reminded me of my son, who served more than a decade ago in the intelligence unit many of them might have belonged to.

articles.title: ‘Sometimes she publishes notes she’s scribbled on her hand’: Édouard Louis on 10 reasons to love Anne Carson
articles.author: Édouard Louis
paras: The French author discovered Carson on a bus while stranded in a snowstorm and has been enthralled by her fearless imagination ever since
‘Delights await!’: Margaret Atwood and other writers on Nobel winner Anne Carson

1. Anne Carson is one of the greatest writers of our time. I discovered her work on a Peter Pan bus from New York to New England. I’d bought Antigonick in a bookstore a few days earlier, almost randomly. From the very first lines, I was enthralled. While we were on the bus, a snowstorm suddenly blanketed the roads, and the other passengers and I found ourselves stuck for 10 hours in rural America, surrounded by an entirely white landscape. I took my computer out of my backpack and started to translate Antigonick into French. Spontaneously. I was so absorbed by the power of Carson’s text that I didn’t notice the hours pass.

2. One of Carson’s greatest strengths is that, unlike so many other contemporary writers, she doesn’t try to “make literature”. She writes. Sometimes clouds do the speaking, in her work, and sometimes monsters do; sometimes, in the middle of a collection of poems, she lets an imaginary Catherine Deneuve take over the narration. Sometimes she writes a letter to her own sleep and sometimes she publishes notes she’s scribbled on her hand. She writes about Homer, but also Rosalía; about Brecht, but also Marilyn Monroe.

articles.title: Why fall yard care could start with doing less – but not nothing
articles.author:
<name>Manjot Kaur Sidhu, Assistant Extension Professor of Horticulture and Ornamental Horticulture Specialist, University of Maine</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/manjot-kaur-sidhu-2746266"/>
paras: Every autumn, homeowners and gardeners tend to engage in a familiar ritual. As trees shed their leaves, people drag out rakes, leaf blowers and lawn bags to strip their yards bare before winter arrives.

It is a tidy habit rooted in aesthetics, but ecologically, clearing away fallen leaves strips the very foundation of local ecosystems. Far from dead debris requiring disposal, this fallen foliage forms a dynamic layer and a biological interface that drives nutrient cycling and is essential for soil health and the environment, including biodiversity .

As a researcher of plant growth in yards and gardens, I would recommend leaving leaves on the ground. There, they can provide essential winter habitat for native pollinators – even in places that don’t have freezing temperatures. And they act as a nutrient-dense, natural mulch for the soil.
Here is the science behind why the first step of fall yard care could simply be doing less – along with practical ways to keep your yard looking neat while nourishing the ecosystem underneath.

To understand why leaf litter matters, it helps to look closely at what happens beneath the surface as temperatures drop. While honeybees pass the winter in sheltered hives , the vast majority of North America’s native pollinators do not.

Up to 70% of native bee species, including many insects’ cocoons and larvae, nest in the ground . Fertilized queen bumblebees burrow just a few inches into the soil or hide under dense leaf mulch to survive the freezing months ahead, to lay eggs in the following spring.
Raking, bagging and blowing leaves away destroys this crucial winter nursery.
Many other insects depend on the shelter of fallen foliage:

Moths and butterflies: Species such as the luna moth ( Actias luna ) and the Isabella tiger moth, whose caterpillar form is the woolly bear , spin cocoons or roll themselves directly inside fallen leaves. Raking or shredding those leaves destroys the next generation.

Fireflies: Adult fireflies lay eggs in moist soil, and their larvae spend up to two years hunting for their food, soft-bodied invertebrates under damp leaf litter . Raking deprives them of moisture and habitat.
Predatory ground beetles : These beneficial predators spend the winter under leaves , emerging in spring to feed on common garden pests such as aphids, slugs and mites.

In addition to being a shelter, fallen leaves are an evolved biological mechanism for nutrient cycling . Trees actively pump vital elements, including calcium, magnesium, potassium and nitrogen from deep subsoils, into their foliage. When autumn comes and leaves drop, these stored nutrients are deposited back into the soil.
Leaving leaves in place triggers fundamental ecological benefits.

A thick blanket of intact leaves acts as a natural insulator for the ground. Air pockets trapped between overlapping leaves moderate the soil temperature and slow heat transfer, buffering against the freeze-thaw cycles that heave soil , fracture plant roots and expose beneficial soil microbes to lethal cold. The intact leaf blanket also conserves moisture and prevents soil from drying out over the winter.

As fungi, earthworms and micro-arthropods digest fallen leaves through late fall and spring, they break down organic matter into a rich material called humus . This slow-release organic fertilizer boosts soil structure, improves water retention in sandy soils, and prevents erosion and runoff in heavy rains .

Decaying leaves feed beneficial mycorrhizal fungi in the soil. Those fungi form symbiotic relationships with plant and tree roots , helping the roots collect water and nutrients from the soil to nourish the plants above. A natural layer of leaves also suppresses spring weed seeds organically without needing synthetic chemical herbicides. And the moist, insulated microclimate under leaf litter is also critical for terrestrial amphibians, including frogs and salamanders , to survive freezing temperatures.

Adopting a softer approach to fall cleanup does not mean your yard has to look completely untamed or that you have to risk killing your lawn . Here is how to balance suburban expectations with sound ecological science:

Move, don’t remove: Move the leaves from lawns and sidewalks, rake them into garden beds, around ornamental plants or into vegetable plots, using manual rakes or electric leaf blowers. Aim for a layer 2 to 3 inches deep. Leaving leaves in grassy areas can help ticks hide there too , but if you move the leaves to garden beds or spots that are used less, the ticks will be less likely to nest in the grass. Establishing pollinator zones on the property can also help reduce tick populations.

Skip the leaf shredder: Mowing over leaves with a mulching mower is better than sending them to landfills, but high-velocity mower blades still kill overwintering insect eggs, chrysalises and larvae. Leave leaves intact wherever possible in plant beds.

Wait for spring to clean up: Do not cut back hollow-stemmed perennials or clear leaf beds during early, warm spring days. Wait until temperatures consistently stay above 50 degrees Fahrenheit (10 degrees Celsius) so overwintering bees and butterflies have time to safely emerge .

When you bag leaves for disposal and then buy commercial wood mulch or synthetic fertilizers in the spring, you are effectively paying a price for what your trees provided for free. By rethinking the cultural expectation of pristine autumn lawns, it’s possible to transform silent landscapes into vibrant habitat sanctuaries, simply by stepping back and allowing natural processes to take over.
