articles.title: How Hurricane Isaias broke through to become the first Atlantic hurricane in an eerily quiet 2026 season
articles.author:
<name>Christopher Davis, Professor of Earth, Geographic, and Climate Sciences, UMass Amherst</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/christopher-davis-2718762"/>
paras: Hurricane Isaias shattered the peace of one of the quietest Atlantic hurricane seasons on record as it grew into 2026’s first Atlantic hurricane and headed for the northern Gulf Coast , with landfall expected late on Oct. 9 or early Oct. 10.

Coastal residents and store owners in Alabama and the Florida Panhandle quickly began boarding up windows and preparing sandbags for damaging wind, rain and storm surge. Tyndall Air Force Base, which suffered severe hurricane damage in 2018, started evacuating fighter jets .

Isaias tied a 1905 storm for the latest-forming first hurricane of a season on record. To understand why it was able to strengthen into a hurricane when no other storms in the first two-thirds of the 2026 season did, let’s take a look at what was going on in the atmosphere.
As an atmospheric scientist who has studied hurricanes for years, I can tell you that wind shear and the climate phenomenon known as El Niño both play important roles.

Usually, Atlantic hurricane activity hits its peak in September . In a typical season, the Atlantic region experiences five hurricanes and two major hurricanes by early October. Having no hurricanes until Oct. 7 is nearly unprecedented in the Atlantic hurricane record.

El Niño is a climate pattern that occurs every few years when ocean surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean heat up. That heat can influence weather around the world – including Atlantic hurricanes.
The 2026 El Niño was already strong by late summer, and forecasters expected to see it become one of the strongest El Niño events on record.

When the waters of the eastern Pacific warm substantially, they create more rising air over the eastern Pacific, and with it, more widespread thunderstorm activity . The net effect is a current of rising air that flows northward across portions of Central America. This flow turns toward the east in the Northern Hemisphere because of the Earth’s rotation , and it increases the westerly winds across the tropical Atlantic.

Winds near the surface blowing from the east, along with winds at higher altitudes blowing from the west, create vertical wind shear . Wind shear makes it harder for hurricanes to form because it disrupts any deep column of moisture that tries to organize into a vortex.

El Niño has another effect on Atlantic hurricane formation: With more rising air above the eastern Pacific warm waters, air tends to subside over the tropical Atlantic and become dry . Hurricanes need lots of moisture, so dry air makes it harder for one to form.
The tropical Atlantic was hit with both vertical wind shear and dry air in 2026.

Most of the storms that managed to form in the Atlantic earlier in 2026 did so to the north of the region of vertical shear and dry air, but it is rare for storms forming at those higher latitudes to become strong hurricanes.
So how did Isaias manage to break through?

First, Isaias did not form in the deep tropics, where many of the strongest hurricanes originate. That region is still seeing plenty of wind shear. Isaias formed over the western Gulf of Mexico (also referred to as the Gulf of America) instead.

In early October, vertical wind shear in the western Gulf weakened and a small region of enhanced moisture moved over the western Gulf. Both of these factors made hurricane formation more likely, and exceptionally warm water provided fuel for the storm that formed.
Isaias organized rapidly in this environment.

But, as is often true with late-season hurricanes approaching the U.S., the jet stream is not far away. While Isaias strengthened, vertical shear also started increasing – not due to El Niño, but because the jet stream tends to dip farther south as autumn sets in.
Isaias grew into a dangerous storm, but it could have been even stronger without the effects of wind shear.
The rapid emergence of Isaias is a reminder that a slow start to the hurricane season doesn’t mean a quiet end. The season does not end officially until November 30.

Atmospheric conditions often change considerably in October from what they were in July through September as temperatures fall. So coastal regions can’t let their guard down yet – the season could bring more surprises.

Christopher Davis works for the University of Massachusetts Amherst, and the NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research. He receives funding from the State of Massachusetts, NASA and the State of California.

articles.title: What we talk about when we talk about US strategic ‘credibility’ – from Vietnam to Iran
articles.author:
<name>Christopher Nichols, Professor of History, Hayes Chair National Security Studies, The Ohio State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/christopher-nichols-1430247"/>
paras: Where has more than seven months of intermittent war , economic threats , stalled diplomacy and promises of a ceasefire in Iran left the concept of U.S. strategic credibility ?
It is a question that political scientists and security and foreign policy experts like us have had to grapple with at each turn of the conflict.
Some commentators have argued that the bombings and multiple ceasefires actually strengthen American credibility by demonstrating American deterrence capabilities and resolve toward adversaries.

Others cite the lack of a persuasive justification for conflict, the strikes themselves and subsequent fits and starts of peacemaking as evidence that America’s global image has been undermined, as has the persuasiveness of its public claims. And this, in turn, has undercut the credibility of future pronouncements by the U.S. administration.

Either way, most observers insist that for the United States, “credibility is on the line in Iran.” But that has long been a central concern of U.S. foreign policy. As political scientist Stephen Walt observed in 2022, one of the most predictable aspects of virtually any debate over Washington’s involvement overseas is the “ ritual invoking of ‘credibility .’”
But what, exactly, is “American credibility”? And why is there apparently so much groupthink about the concept and practice?

For policymakers, diplomats and scholars the technical definition is straightforward: Credibility refers to the perceived likelihood that a country will reliably keeps its promises, carry out its threats and deliver on its pledges. In this manner, a country is credible if allies and adversaries alike will believe it the next time. But as suggested by contemporary debates and usage, credibility, in practice, often means something more than simply keeping up with commitments.

Credibility is not only about whether nations successfully signal resolve, but also whether relevant audiences perceive their commitments as credible. In other words, contemplating a nation’s credibility is about assumptions over the “strategic culture ” that undergird it – and this can include everything from a country’s military resources to abstract notions about its values.
Historical examples are useful here, in particular the Vietnam War, during which American credibility was at stake in unprecedented ways.

On the surface, Vietnam posed little intrinsic value to the United States – it was not a primary theater of the Cold War by most measures. Yet policymakers repeatedly insisted that Vietnam was the place where American credibility had to be demonstrated and established. Why?

Secretary of State John Foster Dulles warned in 1954 that communist expansion in Asia posed “a grave threat to the whole free community” and insisted that demonstrating resolve would prevent greater dangers later. National security adviser McGeorge Bundy similarly argued that the “international prestige of the United States” was deeply invested in Vietnam.
Credibility, to them, meant more than simply honoring commitments. Rather, it was bound up with broader questions of power, honor and America’s place in the world between competing powers.

As diplomatic historian Robert McMahon observed decades ago , credibility has often been treated as if it were a concrete and measurable concept. Yet in practice it has always carried an important symbolic dimension – credibility has come to be a shorthand for American prestige itself.
And that variant of American credibility has in particular rested on anxieties about the continued dominance and superiority of the U.S.-led world order.

During one congressional discussion in 1965, U.S. policymakers warned that withdrawing from Vietnam would mean surrendering “all Asia to Communists,” prompting the reflection : “If a nation with 14 million can make Uncle Sam run, what will China think?”

An exchange between President Lyndon Johnson and Undersecretary of State George Ball in 1965 is even more illustrative. President Johnson worried that abandoning Vietnam would make “all these countries say that Uncle Sam was a paper tiger” and wondered whether America would lose the credibility built by three presidents. Ball’s response was, “No sir. The worst blow would be that the mightiest power on earth is unable to defeat a handful of guerrillas.”
The anxiety was not that America might fail to keep up with its word, but that the leader of the “free world” might fail to defeat a non-Western, technologically inferior opponent.
The credibility at stake was both America’s sense of national self and the perceived superiority of a Western-led world order.

Counterintuitively, while the Vietnam War was fought in the eyes of many policymakers to defend U.S. credibility, its conclusion shattered conventional notions of credibility. It called into question the U.S.’s place in the world in an era historians have termed an “ Age of Fracture ,” characterized by economic challenges such as stagflation, oil shocks and rising distrust in politics, government and institutions.

For many observers within and outside the U.S., images of the helicopters lifting off and fleeing from Saigon – and thereby deserting allies and a purportedly essential cause in the process – signaled a moment of American and Western decline. The phenomenon even led to a widely used term – “ Vietnam Syndrome ” – referring to the public’s unwillingness thereafter to commit to large-scale foreign interventions and nation-building exercises.
That image of U.S. decline and impotence is one that has resonated ever since in foreign policy debates.

The perception of the loss of credibility in Vietnam has served as a yardstick for planning, assessing and implementing interventions in other regions. It has been both a way of warning about the dangers of rash interventionism and the consequences of hubris, as well as a rallying cry to avoid repeating past errors. yet maintain credibility through actions in places from the Middle East to Latin America.

The credibility issues central to the U.S. administration’s actions today in Iran – and Ukraine, Venezuela and elsewhere – are thus about the U.S.’s living up to pledges and following through to achieve objectives. As with Vietnam, they also concern clustering around nebulous concepts. of and aims about not looking weak militarily or diplomatically.

But the Iran example – and particularly the ongoing episodic closures of the Strait of Hormuz – is one of the best illustrations today of how merely invoking credibility to act is not the same as having an overall endgame strategy.

While some commentators view this currently as a sign of a lack of resolve, or credibility, if we turn to Iranian actions and to the words of Iran’s acting Defense Minister Majid Ebn-e-Reza we find something else. Namely, Tehran views all threats from the United States as “ real and credible ” and “as a reason to bolster its defense.”
The U.S. and Iran agree on one thing in terms of credibility: America can credibly be relied on to carry out overwhelming violence.

But the problem, as it was in the Vietnam War, is that credibly engaging in war and violence is not a substitute for strategy. Credibility is affected deeply by strategic cultural assessments about superiority and inferiority, and notions about when, where, how and for whom the credibility matters.

Moreover, merely establishing credibility to act cannot necessarily overwhelm a resolute adversary, as has been borne out in Iran. In fact, it can also perpetuate never-ending conflict that serves to undermine the very prestige and world power that it was supposed to enhance.

articles.title: When abortion and surrogacy law collide, contracts can’t answer the hardest questions
articles.author:
<name>Sonia Suter, Professor of Law, George Washington University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/sonia-suter-1303960"/>
paras: Surrogacy arrangements – agreements for someone to carry a pregnancy for the intended parents – have existed for millennia , and modern surrogacy contracts for half a century .

These contracts typically address parental rights, the possibility of abortion , medical instructions, health insurance and payment of expenses , each side with its own legal representation . The contracts are usually honored, resulting in thousands of babies born through surrogacy in the U.S., at a cost that can top US$200,000 when agencies are involved.

In a 2026 case, surrogate McKenna West refused the intended parents’ request for an abortion after the fetus was diagnosed with a serious heart condition. The case raises an uncomfortable question: What happens when the surrogate’s bodily autonomy collides with the intended parents’ wishes?

As scholars of reproductive justice and family law , we see this case as an example of how rapidly changing abortion laws, reproductive technology and family law can create conflicts that surrogacy contracts cannot necessarily anticipate.

West’s contract stated that “there shall be a termination of the pregnancy for a fetal abnormality … if the Intended Parents request” it. She later wrote that “their lawyer and my own former lawyer sent me letters threatening six-figure penalties if I didn’t comply with their demand to terminate.”

Instead, West moved from Alaska to Texas, where she had family support and believed the baby, when born, could get needed care . Moreover, she knew that Texas bans abortion in almost all circumstances. Meanwhile, the intended parents, who lived in California, obtained a court order before the birth stating they would become the legal parents once the baby was born.

Before West gave birth, the Texas attorney general obtained a court order requiring lifesaving care for the baby, stating that “the intended parents have refused to agree that they will consent to the lifesaving surgery.” West sought custody but was willing to drop her claims if the couple agreed to the baby’s treatment .

After the Texas courts upheld the intended parents’ rights, West asked the Supreme Court to intervene so she could receive “further information about the child she carried for 37 weeks and fought to save.” The court declined , leaving West no rights to the baby .

In a similar 2012 case, surrogate Crystal Kelley signed a contract allowing the intended parents to call for an abortion in case of a severe fetal abnormality. When the fetus was diagnosed with a heart defect and other serious anomalies, the parents asked Kelley to terminate the pregnancy. She refused and left Connecticut, where she would not have had parental rights, for Michigan, which at the time would treat her as the legal mother. Kelley placed the baby for adoption, and the girl’s adoptive parents raised her until her death at 8 .

In the 1988 Baby M case , a surrogate who was also the genetic mother insisted she should be the mother despite signing a contract to relinquish parental rights. The New Jersey Supreme Court voided that contract because it held that she could not give up her parental rights before birth. As a result, it recognized the surrogate as the legal mother but awarded custody to the father. She later received visitation rights .
Surrogacy contracts establishing legal parentage are enforceable in a number of states . But surrogacy laws vary by state, creating a patchwork with respect to enforceability .

West’s journey, for example, involved three states – Alaska, Texas and the intended parents’ state of California. They are deemed surrogacy-friendly , meaning contracts are relatively easy to enforce there, though the states diverge sharply on abortion.

Surrogacy agreements may require the surrogate to restrict travel, eat nutritiously and cooperate with healthcare providers. As in the West and Kelley cases, agreements may also specify when the surrogate could be asked to abort or, if pregnant with multiple fetuses, selectively terminate.
These abortion provisions have rarely been tested in court, and West’s case hasn’t resolved whether they are enforceable. Rather, they raise the question: Can anyone be forced to have an abortion?

After the Supreme Court’s 2022 Dobbs decision , which held there is no fundamental right to abortion, states have determined their own abortion laws. In states like Texas, abortion provisions in surrogacy contracts are unenforceable. But even where abortion is legal, a court would likely refuse to compel an abortion , given the surrogate’s bodily autonomy.
A surrogate’s control over her body may be more limited, however, when intended parents seek to enforce provisions meant to protect the fetus.

If a physician recommends a C-section for the fetus’s well-being and the surrogate refuses, for example, a court might enforce a contract clause requiring her “to cooperate with her medical providers.”
Even before 2022 , when abortion was still a federal constitutional right, courts in some – but not all – jurisdictions ordered C-sections against the pregnant person’s wishes.
In other words, bodily autonomy has never been absolute for pregnant people.
Since Dobbs, surrogacy and abortion have become increasingly intertwined.

In 2025, a Florida judge questioned the constitutionality of surrogacy on fetal-personhood grounds – the legal theory that an unborn fetus or embryo has the same legal rights as a born human – even as he granted the intended parents parental rights.

In his view , there can be no “contractual ownership interest over the unborn baby.” Florida’s attorney general took the argument further, declaring that the couple’s contract with the surrogate violated the 13th Amendment’s ban on slavery . A spokesperson said he was concerned “about any case where a surrogacy company profits off the sale of children.”

Some conservative legislators and advocacy groups have also been challenging the legitimacy of surrogacy, a few with plans to limit or even ban it . Consequently, in states that take fetal and embryo personhood seriously, surrogacy contracts and even IVF could become unavailable.

West’s case has surfaced starkly different views of what is at stake. For some, surrogacy is a form of baby selling that should not be allowed. For others, it is a way for intended parents to create families and for surrogates to support them.

Surrogacy asks the law to recognize both the interests of people who intend to become parents and the autonomy of the person who is pregnant. Dobbs has made that balance harder to maintain by inviting fetal-personhood principles into areas of law that had not previously treated fetuses or embryos as persons.

articles.title: The oil market that sets today’s gas prices was invented in western Pennsylvania
articles.author:
<name>Brian C. Black, Distinguished Professor of History and Environmental Studies, Penn State</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/brian-c-black-193343"/>
paras: The fall of 2026 is a moment of energy centrality, when geopolitics unfolding far away shows up in Americans’ everyday lives.
In Pennsylvania, the statewide diesel price averages US$6.50 per gallon. In Iowa, farmers are paying more than $6 a gallon for diesel. And in Alaska, unleaded gas runs more than $9 a gallon .

As a distinguished professor of history and environmental studies at Penn State Altoona , I write widely about oil and energy issues . This moment has me thinking about how the oil industry began nearly 170 years ago in northwestern Pennsylvania.

In 1859, Edwin Drake struck oil along Oil Creek near Titusville, Pennsylvania. His well was funded by investors from New Bedford, Massachusetts, who were looking for a replacement for whale oil, which was expensive and challenging to acquire.

The first oil deals were struck on the streets of Oil City, about 90 miles north of Pittsburgh, while traders were still working out basic questions about “rock oil,” as crude was then called: What was it good for, and how much should it cost?

To create a more formal system, the oil traders developed a railroad car designed to be a rolling oil exchange on the Oil Creek Railway. It made 13 stops daily between Titusville and Oil City, and trading was conducted on the honor system, with no written certificates of purchase or sale.
As the industry quickly grew , an oil exchange office was set up in the Arlington Hotel in Oil City.

Traders pushed for a building of their own, arguing that a growing industry needed a more formal market. By 1874, Pennsylvania’s Oil Valley was producing roughly 30,000 barrels of crude oil a day, which sold for an average of about $1.15 a barrel.

Rather than physically moving barrels around, trading had moved from handshakes to paper. Pipelines issued certificates representing the oil in their lines. Traders bought and sold the paper certificates representing oil, often trading the same barrels many times in a single day. As a result, the volume of oil changing hands could reach 10 million to 14 million barrels a day, hundreds of times more than the wells actually produced.
In April 1874, a group of Oil City oil men received a state charter to form the Oil City Oil Exchange. Construction started in July 1877 at the corner of Center and Seneca streets.

When the Oil Exchange opened in April 1878, the local newspaper called it “the largest and most elaborate structure ever erected in the Oil Region.” The building, the paper said, reflected how big the speculative side of the oil trade had become. Standard Oil, the nation’s largest oil company at the time , owned by John D. Rockefeller, kept offices in the building.
The Oil City Oil Exchange heavily influenced early crude oil pricing. Brokers there collected 10 cents a barrel from buyers and 5 cents from sellers.

While the Oil City Oil Exchange was the center of the oil industry for nearly two decades, by 1895 Standard Oil had effectively cornered the market. Its chief buyer, Titusville resident Joseph Seep, began paying producers cash directly, at a price Standard set itself. That control lasted until 1911, when the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in a landmark antitrust case that the trust had to be broken into 34 separate companies.
After that, no single company controlled the price of crude oil.
Predicting oil prices became a much bigger concern after the oil crises of the 1970s , when sudden price hikes rattled economies around the world.

Today, the price of crude oil is set largely by traders on two exchanges : the New York Mercantile Exchange and the Intercontinental Exchange. Prices there shift from second to second, and gas prices at the pump follow them, usually within days or weeks.

Much of that trading involves futures contracts, which are agreements to buy oil at a set price on a future date. In the U.S., the benchmark contract is for oil delivered to Cushing, Oklahoma, a storage hub where many of the country’s pipelines meet.

The latest shock to that system began this year. War began on Feb. 28, 2026, when the U.S. and Israel launched airstrikes on Iranian military targets that killed Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Iran struck back with missiles and drones and began attacking commercial ships in the waters around the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow channel between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula that connects the Persian Gulf to the open ocean.
Within days, the attacks and a wave of canceled shipping insurance brought tanker traffic nearly to a halt.

On March 2, a Revolutionary Guard commander made the closure official in a statement carried by Iran’s state media : “The Strait of Hormuz is closed. If anyone tries to pass, the heroes of the Revolutionary Guards and the regular navy will set those ships ablaze.”
Roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil normally passes through the strait. Most of it goes to Asia, not the U.S. But because oil is traded on a global market, prices rose everywhere .

Oil and gas prices kept climbing as peace talks failed. By May 2026, the average price of a gallon of regular gas in the U.S. was 50% higher than before the war began. Since then, Gulf oil producers have found ways around the blockade , sending oil through pipelines to ports outside the strait and through a U.S.-guarded shipping route near Oman. By late September, those work-arounds had restored about half of the oil that normally passes through the strait, helping keep crude prices around $100 a barrel instead of the much higher levels many analysts had feared.

Oil City’s exchange building is long gone. It was torn down in 1926 to make way for a bank. But the market its traders built, where paper claims on oil change hands far faster than the oil itself moves, still sets what drivers pay at the pump in Oil City and everywhere else.

articles.title: Why faculty diversity at universities still lags far behind the changing demographics of college students
articles.author:
<name>Rodney Coates, Professor of Critical Race and Ethnic Studies, Miami University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/rodney-coates-1431026"/>
paras: U.S. colleges and universities have long struggled to increase the racial diversity of their faculty.

And after they are hired, some faculty of color say they feel that their qualifications and scholarship are subjected to greater scrutiny, or that they do not feel valued by their colleagues and schools.

As a scholar of critical race theory , I have studied these barriers, and I think that it is helpful to understand what universities, students and academic research all stand to gain from a more diverse faculty.
While college faculties have become more racially diverse since the 1970s, the diversification of the faculty has not kept pace with changes in the college student population.
Overall, approximately 16% of the U.S. population were of color in 1970.
In 1975, approximately 8% of full-time faculty at U.S. colleges and universities were people of color. Approximately 4% were Black , 2% were Asian, and 1% were Hispanic.
In 1976, meanwhile, nearly 16% of U.S. college students were people of color .
Black students specifically accounted for about 9% of all full-time college students in 1976, Hispanic students about 4% and Asian or Pacific Islander students about 2%.

By 2022, 72% of full-time faculty across universities and colleges nationwide were white, while Asian professors made up 13%, Black professors 7% and Hispanic professors 6%, according to the National Center for Education Statistics.
By 2022, Hispanic students accounted for 21.5% of U.S.-resident students at colleges and universities, Black students 13.2% and Asian students 7.8%.
Overall, in 2022, people of color made up approximately 41% of the U.S. population.
Diversifying college faculties has not been a straightforward journey in recent years.
After a white police officer shot and killed Michael Brown, a Black teenager living in Ferguson, Missouri , in 2014, student protests erupted across college campuses .
Amid this student activism around racism, some U.S. research universities publicly committed to making their faculties more diverse .
By 2015, at least 88 of the country’s 187 leading research universities had promised to take this step .
Another 96 schools made similar commitments over the next few years, including after the 2020 police murder of George Floyd , a Black man living in Minneapolis.
Among a group of selected research universities examined by The Washington Post , the share of Black, Hispanic and other underrepresented faculty rose from 9% in 2015 to 12% in 2024.

But many of those public efforts have since been scaled back or abandoned. Of the 184 universities that had made faculty-diversity commitments, at least 108 had fully or partially rolled them back by early 2026.

Separately, in 2023, more than 45 bills meant to restrict or ban diversity, equity and inclusion efforts in higher education were introduced in state legislatures. By late that year, eight states had enacted anti-DEI laws.
These measures have included restrictions on schools’ DEI offices and programs, diversity statements and spending on DEI-related initiatives.
Some scholars argue that these policies, along with other restrictions on racial-equity programs and initiatives, are contributing to what they describe as the “resegregation” of higher education.

Some faculty of color have said that they have seen evidence of a kind of tokenism in higher education. Some feel that they are expected to represent, exemplify, teach and do research with a focus on race and ethnic studies programs.

“Apparently, my colleague had assumed that because I am Black, I must be an expert on the African diaspora,” wrote Tyler Austin Harper, a former environmental studies professor at Bates College, in an August 2026 article in The Atlantic, which detailed his decision to leave his tenure-track position.

“The school’s culture encouraged us to see professors of color as vehicles for achieving the college’s diversity goals. The inescapable conclusion I arrived at was that I had been hired to be visibly Black first and a scholar second, if at all,” Harper wrote.
Other faculty of color have reported feeling like they and their scholarship are undervalued by their schools and peers.
Some faculty of color also report that scholarship focusing on marginalized populations or social problems is treated as less rigorous or less central to their disciplines.
Faculty of color across American colleges and universities face other challenges , including feeling isolated or like they are being watched .
Some faculty of color also report feeling like they should mentor students of color . This work can add to their workloads and, they say, sometimes come at a cost to their own careers.
Some research has found racial disparities in tenure and promotion outcomes , although those disparities vary considerably by discipline, school, gender and racial or ethnic group.
LGBTQ+ faculty of color, in particular, also report feeling isolated or intimidated, and experiencing delayed tenure or other promotion opportunities .
Having diverse faculty can benefit students and universities in several ways.
Research has linked greater faculty diversity to a range of positive outcomes for students, including student retention and college completion, particularly for Black and Hispanic students.
Exposure to professors with different backgrounds and perspectives can broaden students’ educational experiences.
Having a diverse faculty at universities can also strengthen academic research.
Researchers’ backgrounds can influence the questions they ask, the populations they study and how participants respond to them.
More diverse research teams can also bring different experiences and perspectives to the design and interpretation of research.

Research teams and study populations that lack diversity can overlook important perspectives and produce findings that are less applicable to broader populations. Conversely, more diverse teams can bring a wider range of perspectives and approaches to research.
I believe that continuing to make university faculty ranks more diverse is essential for higher education.

This is not simply a matter of making professors more closely resemble the students they teach. It is about broadening the perspectives represented in classrooms and research, and ensuring that universities draw on the widest possible pool of scholars and ideas.

articles.title: Your digital photos and posts are scattered everywhere: This startup ties them all together
articles.author: John Cook
paras: Eluum is taking aim at a problem created by the explosion of digital life: We chronicle our lives everywhere, but a single home for our most meaningful memories is hard to come by.

The Seattle startup’s new app brings together photos, videos, social posts, locations and other personal moments from across the digital landscape, using AI to help organize them into an evolving record of a person’s life, a feature it calls MyLifeStory.

The bootstrapped company, founded by former Microsoft and Avalara manager Bilkay Rose , former Microsoft software engineer Dale Rector and former investor relations exec Jennifer Gianola , sees an opportunity to create what it calls a user-controlled “memory layer” for social media.
The idea grew out of Rose’s own struggle to piece together years of family memories across a variety of platforms and devices. The app is available for iOS , Android and the web .
We caught up with Rose, who is part of the CoMotion entrepreneurial community at the University of Washington, for the latest installment of GeekWire’s Startup Spotlight.
In 50 words or less, give us your elevator pitch :

Eluum is building the future of social around people’s stories. MyLifeStory brings scattered photos, videos, social posts, places, and personal context into one evolving life story, helped by Lumi, our artificial intelligence memory companion, and controlled by the person whose life it represents.
What problem are you obsessed with solving?

Each of us creates thousands of digital artifacts, but they are scattered across camera rolls, social platforms, devices, and feeds. Nothing brings them together as the evolving story of a person’s life. Every person I know deals with this issue, but it seems too big to solve for most. We believe technology has finally reached the point where MyLifeStory can become real: a living story built across time, not another temporary feed built around advertising and engagement.
What surprised you after talking to customers?

People do not need another place to post. They want help making sense of what they have already created, and continue to create on a daily basis. What surprised us was how consistently people described feeling overwhelmed by their digital lives. They have the photos and posts, but the meaning — the people they actually create memories with, places they visit, experiences, and stories connecting everything — is being lost every single day.
How has artificial intelligence changed the way you build your company?

Artificial intelligence gives a small, determined team extraordinary leverage. It allows Dale, our CTO, and our broader team to build, design, test, and learn faster without requiring a massive organization or budget. More importantly, it makes our product possible.

Lumi helps users organize disconnected moments, add context, and gradually shape them into meaningful life stories. Artificial intelligence is the helper; the person remains the author. We have a bold vision for what technology can do for the average person, and we believe the first problem to solve is our memories. The most important thing in everyone’s lives is their journey through life.
What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?
People sometimes assume Eluum is another social network or photo-storage application. It is neither. Eluum is building a human memory layer for social.

Our integrated social tools help people manage and share content, but MyLifeStory is the destination: a private, user-controlled story of their life that becomes more valuable over time. As a female founder, my mission is to build a company that can solve real problems. Our mission is to solve problems and make our users’ lives better.
What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Our founding team had to decide whether Eluum was primarily a life-memory platform or an integrated social platform. We see two enormous problems: social media needs a new, human-centered model decoupling our social lives from ad and algorithmic platforms, and people need a way to preserve their fragmented digital lives.

We ultimately realized these ideas are connected. Integrated social is how moments flow into Eluum; MyLifeStory is what gives those moments lasting meaning. Balancing that product vision with limited resources — while continually asking what users truly want, need, and would think is genuinely exciting — remains our hardest discipline.
What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?
Do not confuse limited resources with an inability to make progress. A determined small team, the right technology, and a meaningful problem can accomplish far more than most people expect.
Listen closely to users, but maintain enough conviction to build what they cannot yet describe. Think big and don’t get easily discouraged early on. Prove your idea.

I cannot imagine declaring that we have “made it.” That would be naive because trust must continually be earned. Success would mean Eluum becomes a trusted brand people rely on to build and preserve their life stories, knowing our products were designed to work for them, protect what matters, and become more meaningful with time.

articles.title: Microsoft responds to White House immigration crackdown as Trump honors Nadella
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: The Trump administration suspended Microsoft from the federal program the company uses to help foreign workers stay in the U.S. permanently, accusing the tech giant of abusing the system.

The announcement by Vice President JD Vance, during a news conference Thursday morning at the White House, came hours before President Trump gave Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella the National Medal of Technology and Innovation in a ceremony honoring Elon Musk and other tech leaders.

Vance said Microsoft laid off 6,000 American workers last year while getting 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards, which he said amounted to replacing U.S. employees with lower-paid foreign workers.

“There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft,” Vance said at the news conference, while adding, “Our message to Microsoft is you’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers.”

Microsoft’s response: In a statement , the company said 80% of the roughly 6,000 H-1B applications it filed last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of people who already work for the company. The rest were for new hires who were already living in the U.S. legally, a group equal to about 1% of its U.S. workforce.
“They are not new arrivals to our country,” the company said.

Microsoft said it pays H-1B employees “the same as any other employees doing comparable work,” that its wages are “among the highest of all H-1B filings,” and that the vast majority of its U.S. employees are Americans.
The statement didn’t mention the suspension, but the company said it looks forward to “providing the Administration with additional information.”

Details of the penalty: The suspension covers the Labor Department’s Permanent Labor Certification program , known as PERM. It’s usually the first step when a company sponsors a foreign employee to live and work in the U.S. permanently. To get approved, the employer has to advertise the job and show the government that no qualified American worker was available.

Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the department won’t accept new applications from Microsoft or process the ones it already has pending. The move doesn’t stop Microsoft from applying for H-1B visas, the temporary work visas that many PERM applicants hold.
The department also suspended Adobe and six IT outsourcing firms: Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini.

Trump didn’t mention the suspension at the ceremony. Introducing Nadella, he credited him with making Microsoft “an early leader in superintelligence” and said, “Satya, we are honored to give you the National Medal of Technology and Innovation. It is so well deserved.”

The official citation honored Nadella “for his transformative leadership of a critical American technology company” and for building the “hyperscale infrastructure that enabled the training and global deployment of American superintelligence.”
Tech industry reaction: The announcement drew pushback in Seattle’s tech community.

“There has been a continuous, nonstop deluge of immigration-related news leading up to the midterms,” said Xiao Wang , co-founder and CEO of Boundless , a Seattle startup that helps people navigate the U.S. immigration process.

Wang pushed back on Vance’s characterization of H-1B workers as “foreign indentured servants,” noting there are wage requirements to prevent underpayment of employees. He emphasized the economic benefits of educating and employing the students and workers who seek these visas — and what happens if they’re discouraged or prevented from coming to the U.S.
“What I have been trying to warn folks about is the long-term chilling effects that would be detrimental to the long-term prosperity and competitiveness of the United States,” he said.

Wang said the idea that the layoffs and recruitment of foreign-born workers are linked doesn’t make sense. “Layoffs and hiring are not one for ones of each other, especially at giant companies like Microsoft,” he said.
Someone laid off from a gaming division at Microsoft isn’t interchangeable, for example, with an H-1B employee who’s an expert in agentic AI for a Copilot role, he said.

Priyanka Kulkarni , founder and CEO of the immigration technology company Casium , previously worked at Microsoft for more than a decade building enterprise AI technology. She personally navigated H-1B status before becoming a permanent resident.

“I worked alongside people from around the world whose expertise helped build technology used by American businesses every day,” she said, adding, “America wants to lead in AI. That requires attracting and retaining exceptional people, and giving them confidence that they can build a future here.”
Kulkarni called the phrase “foreign indentured servants” troubling, and said it exposes a contradiction in the administration’s action.

“If the concern is that workers depend too heavily on their employers, blocking their path to permanent residency could deepen that dependence,” she said. “Permanent residency gives people more freedom to change jobs, negotiate pay, and start businesses.”

articles.title: Rocket fuel: Seattle-area startups raise a record $3.5B as national VC funding cools
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Seattle-area startups raised $3.5 billion in venture capital in the third quarter, the most in any quarter going back at least a decade, led by big rounds for Kent-based rocket maker Stoke Space , Bellevue developer platform Temporal and Everett fusion company Helion .

That’s more than triple the $1 billion raised in the region in the same quarter a year earlier, according to the PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor . It’s also more than $1 billion above the previous quarterly high of about $2.4 billion, reached in late 2018 and again in late 2022.

Most of the money went to a handful of companies building physical things: rockets, satellites, spacecraft and fusion power plants. Three space companies in the region raised $1.6 billion combined: Stoke, Redmond-based Starcloud and Seattle’s Hubble Network .

Nationally, the trend went the other way. U.S. venture funding fell 40% from the prior quarter, to $98.4 billion, as the giant rounds for frontier AI labs that drove the first half of the year tapered off.

Seattle ranked seventh among U.S. metro areas for venture dollars in the quarter. The Bay Area led with $40.7 billion, followed by Los Angeles, New York, Austin, Boston and Denver. Denver’s $4.2 billion came largely from a single $3.9 billion round for AI data center developer Crusoe.
By number of deals, Seattle ranked eighth, with 94.

The total includes Helion’s $500 million round, which the company announced in June but PitchBook counts in the third quarter. Even without it, the quarter would still be the region’s biggest on record.

articles.title: Pollet and Dreher Hone Their Pitch to Urbanists in LD46 Race
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Depending how the November election goes, the residents of the 46th Legislative District in Northwest Seattle could have a new state representative after Rep. Gerry Pollet drew a relatively strong challenge from former federal prosecutor Will Dreher. Dreher has staked his campaign on a bid to lead the charge for artificial intelligence regulations, while Pollet is leaning on his experience, and his campaign has pitched him as the real progressive in the race.
In a three-way race, Pollet finished the primary on top, with 51.6% of the primary vote. Dreher won nearly 31% and has serious ground to close if he hopes to pull off the upset.

Plus, the dynamic of the race got a little weird after the primary. Tech entrepreneur and progressive rabblerouser Ron Davis, who The Urbanist Election Committee (on which I serve) endorsed , was eliminated after pulling in 16% of the vote. Rather than endorsing the other challenger or simply riding off into the sunset, Davis enthusiastically endorsed Pollet , and took to sharply attacking Dreher and defending Pollet via two long posts on his website, Rondevous .

Also catching criticism from Davis was The Stranger , which endorsed Dreher in the primary. "Let’s unleash this blue-blooded Yankee on the billionaire tech lobby that writes our laws in Olympia," The Stranger wrote. That endorsement likely sealed Davis' loss, although the gulf between the candidates was large enough he may have lost anyway.

"I came back to the same inexorable conclusion I reached in early July: that The Stranger's endorsements really are that powerful, and that it's nearly impossible for a progressive to overcome its influence even with a strong campaign and a lot of grassroots support," Davis wrote in August.

After his primary loss, Davis alleged Pollet – despite his earlier decision to challenge him for his seat – wasn't so bad, and was actually a standout on a number of issues, including education and progressive taxation.

The move came as a surprise to some urbanists who tracked Pollet's anti-urbanist positions early in his career, such as opposing bike lanes in Wedgwood and obstructing statewide housing reform. In contrast, Dreher is a regular cyclist and has pledged to be a reliable pro-housing vote.

"I bike commuted for about four or five years after the pandemic started downtown from my house in Ravenna, and you know one of the things that I very quickly learned as a bike commuter was, I mean, for me personally at least, that I was not comfortable biking with traffic," Dreher told The Urbanist . "And that the number one thing for both safety and to increase the actual uptake of biking seems to have obviously not just protected bike lanes, but protected bike trails and making sure that we have a robust connected trail network."

Dreher said the state should invest more in transit and pursue congestion pricing to make roads work better for all, following in the footsteps of New York City's new highly successful congestion pricing system in Lower Manhattan.

"Manhattan is a very small island in the grand scheme of things relative to the population of New York City," Dreher said. "Downtown Seattle is a land constrained area, with only so many ways to get in or out, and congestion pricing - it's true - is useful for and can be used for raising revenue, but you know I view its primary purpose as modifying behavior in a way that helps the fight against climate change, right? And in a way that helps make our downtown both less congested, have less local pollution, and in general be helping to encourage folks to use alternative ways to get downtown."
While he granted it would take time, Dreher expressed interest in being part of a coalition advancing congestion pricing.

"The good thing is that we now have some cities that are actually exploring, and not just exploring in theory, but actually in practice using congestion pricing, and the sky has not fallen," Dreher said. "My hope would be that we can start to build a coalition around what I think is a fairly sensible policy solution that more cities in the United States should be using. [...] It's something that I think makes a ton of sense. It's something that I think we just need to start having that conversation now in order to make it become a reality at some point in the near future."

On housing issues, Dreher told The Urbanist he is interested in pursuing a statewide funded inclusionary zoning program and in exploring a land value tax. He also pledged to be a reliable vote on housing abundance, although his campaign website did formerly use some "neighborhood character"-type language that Davis portrayed as dog whistles for "not in my backyard" (NIMBY) housing opponents. Dreher has since removed the language and told The Urbanist that it was an honest mistake, rather than a dog whistle.

Dreher's linguistic choices aside, Pollet was such an obstacle as chair of the House Local Government Committee that I named him to the "zeroes" list in our annual legislative recap after the 2021 and 2022 sessions.
Davis himself noted the cost of delays from housing reform holdouts like Pollet when in his campaign rollout interview with The Urbanist back in March.

“Those years were low-interest-rate years. We could have tens of thousands, maybe 50,000 or 100,000 more modestly-priced homes in the region right now, and they would be bidding over us, instead of us bidding over what’s left. And that’s a really huge and ugly, frustrating dynamic,” Davis told The Urbanist at the time.

That frustration seemed to extend to members of the Democratic caucus, who removed Pollet as chair following the 2022 session. Democrats came back in 2023 and finally succeeded in passing statewide middle housing reform via House Bill 1110. That law recently bore fruit as the mandate kicked in last year in many cities, including Seattle , which finally phased out restrictive single family zoning and allowed fourplexes or greater citywide after more than a decade of flirting with the idea to no avail.

Pollet ended up voting for HB 1110, but not before pressing his colleagues to pass an amendment allowing up to a quarter of an affected city's residential land to be carved out of rezones by citing displacement risk. In practice, the logistics of the displacement-risk carveouts have proven complicated enough that most cities have avoided them.

Fast forward to 2026 and Pollet has the endorsement of some of the legislature's most well-known urbanists, like Rep. Julia Reed (D-36th LD, Queen Anne), and Nicole Macri and Shaun Scott (D-43rd LD, Capitol Hill).

"I know I've evolved," Pollet told The Urbanist during an interview last month. "It's important to evolve and learn and realize that I wasn't as steeped in it as I needed to be on some aspects of middle housing, I was much more focused on housing issues relating to multifamily and transit-oriented development than middle housing."

Pollet portrayed himself as better at spotting when local activists were simply making excuses, rather than raising genuine concerns, such as the frequent excuse that neighborhoods need more robust infrastructure before they can accept housing growth, whether beefier roads or utilities or bigger schools.

"One of the things I learned is that listening to people who said, 'Well, we don't have the infrastructure,' was a NIMBY response that we needed to say, 'We're going to force you to have the infrastructure if you truly don't.' But we're not just going to take your word for it because it's often a NIMBY response, and that's an example of where I feel I was very conscious of my changing position that we have to force local governments to do that."

In illustrating how he's evolved and become an asset for the urbanist coalition that rattled off a string of policy wins in recent legislative sessions, Pollet pointed out he helped ensure that statewide parking reform passed in 2025 .

"I not only voted for it, but when it came to the floor of the House, we were briefed on it in caucus, and it ran into a roadblock that nearly pulled it from the schedule," Pollet said, before launching into a story about he helped broker an agreement between his colleagues and disability rights advocates to ensure those concerns did not derail the parking reform bill.

Davis, who met with The Urbanist along with Pollet last month shortly after endorsing him, vouched for his former rival, saying he was a big help in passing parking reform, which Davis was lobbying for on behalf of the Sightline Institute. (Of course, not so helpful overall that he opted against challenging him for his seat.)

Given his background, Pollet is naturally sympathetic to environmental concerns and is skeptical of efforts to streamline the State Environmental Policy Act, which has been criticized as a needless hurdle for housing projects, often hijacked by degrowth activists and NIMBYs to delay projects. Pollet's roots and his road to politics are in environmental law.

"I went to law school at the UW to be an environmental public interest attorney," Pollet told The Urbanist during a September interview. "[I] led the effort to stop Hanford from being a high-level nuclear waste dump, working with the Yakima [Tribe] to protect Gable Mountain, which is sacred to them, and ran the statewide ballot initiative to stop that in 1986, and then founded the organization leading work on the cleanup of Hanford, and along the way, you know, I was very active on many of our groundbreaking environmental laws in the state, including helping draft the Growth Management Act. I was one of the five or six authors of our state Superfund law model, and lobbied on many many environmental laws and helped pass many of them in our state."
Dreher, like Davis, is a Harvard Law trained attorney. Dreher followed in the footsteps of his father, who was a top environmental lawyer for the Clinton and Obama administrations.

Dreher famously clerked for Brett Kavanaugh , the Trump-nominated judge who won a lifetime appointment on the U.S. Supreme Court in 2018. Dreher signed a letter of support for that bid, along with fellow former law clerks. Davis used that as a frequent attack line on the campaign trail, but it didn't seem to fully resonate with voters, given the primary result.

After Kavanaugh's Supreme Court nomination happened in 2018 and the sexual assault allegations against him came out, Dreher said he changed his mind and withdrew his support. Dreher later that year signed onto a second letter supporting an FBI investigation of the allegations.

In 2019, Dreher joined the Department of Justice under the Trump administration as an Assistant U.S. Attorney in the Western District of Washington. His website notes "Dreher has the rare distinction of having prosecuted 25 January 6th insurrectionists." He spent over five years as a federal prosecutor, before leaving to join private practice as a litigator at the firm Keller Rohrback.

Dreher helped lead the firm's artificial intelligence litigation group and was appointed Co-Lead Interim Class Counsel in the copyright infringement class action Hendrix et al. v. Apple, Inc . The case alleges copyright infringement over texts Apple fed into its large language model or LLM, without permission from the authors or publishers.
Dreher has made reining in AI platforms and the tech giants behind them as a centerpiece of his campaign.

"The primary impetus for me getting in this particular race now was really just how rapidly accelerating, I think, our challenges with artificial intelligence and technology more broadly," Dreher said. "So like data privacy, mass surveillance, social media use with kids. There were just a number of tech issues that I've been working on in my current job for the last couple of years, but that I just had seen very little progress on at the state legislature, and I think even beyond that, very little focus on those issues."

Dreher pointed out that the Trump administration seemed to be going in the opposite direction, embracing a rapid expansion of AI applications for short-term financial gain. The state, meanwhile, has been flatfooted when it comes to regulating AI, in his estimation.

"My daughter, who's nine, always talks about how she wants to be a teacher when she grows up," Dreher said. "And Melania Trump in March, came out and had a rollout with a robot teacher and said, 'This will be the future of education.' And I'd say that was really the moment where it fully clicked or crystallized – that I just felt like I needed to do something to try to make sure that that was not the future of education, and more broadly, to try to kickstart or jumpstart our state to start taking seriously that battle."

On the other hand, Dreher's critics – with Davis at the vanguard – have questioned whether Dreher is ready to take on the tech giants so heavily invested in infusing AI into American life. They've pointed out that employees at the AI firm Anthropic were a top source of donations for Dreher's campaign, much of that money from out of state. Pollet, himself, seemed to take offense that Dreher was seeking to claim ownership of education reform, AI, and data privacy regulation issues, which he saw the state legislature as already making significant headway on.

"My thought is same thing goes as education. How would he know? He's not lobbied one day on these issues in Olympia," Pollet told The Urbanist . "There are legislators who know a lot more than him about those issues, and like part of that is the data center issues, right? And you know, he started this campaign, and I don't think he knew that I and others, working with [Rep.] Beth Doglio, had introduced what is viewed nationally as a model bill in terms of regulating data centers. And on data privacy, I don't think he knows, for example, what the battle has been in this state, and we have really strong champions on data privacy."
While not as versed in urbanist bread-and-butter topics as Davis, Dreher still sees himself as the standard-bearer for those issues now that Davis has been knocked out of the race.

"I frankly appreciate Ron's expertise and experience on a number of the issues that we've talked about, housing and transit issues in particular," Dreher said. "I was happy that that was one of the focuses in the race, and I intend to continue to make it a focus for the rest of the race. But now... the voters maybe have a somewhat simplified decision to make between myself and Representative Pollet."

articles.title: What the Seattle Parks ‘Healthy Capitol Hill Hike’ fitness equipment for people and dogs looks like
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Seattle Parks and Recreation has officially debuted the Healthy Capitol Hill Hike , an outdoor fitness initiative allowing neighborhood residents and their dogs to work out together across Capitol Hill.
CHS reported here on the initiative touted earlier this year by the city as part of activation efforts to help address public safety issues in parks across Capitol Hill and the Central District.

Seattle Parks has not said what the total budget for the installations tallies up to but said it was planned to keep costs minimal and draw on existing resources. Infrastructure ranges from heavy duty parks-style human workout equipment seen in public spaces across the country to a row of poles now installed in the middle of Broadway Hill Park as a dog agility station.

The low-budget project adds human- and dog-friendly fitness equipment alongside bodyweight workout stations to eight neighborhood green spaces, including Broadway Hill , Tashkent Park, Seven Hills Park, Summit Slope Park, and Williams Place . Designed through local community feedback, the effort aims to boost park safety and neighborhood accessibility.

Starting at Cal Anderson Park , visitors can choose between a 1.6-mile loop featuring upper-body exercise recommendations or a 1.5-mile loop focused on lower-body movements. Walkers and runners can also link both paths together for a complete 5K course. Digital route maps and suggested workouts are available online from seattle.gov .

articles.title: 19 Capitol Hill and Central District organizations and businesses join call for Seattle to move $8M in budget from hiring more cops to spending more on artists
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: More than 600 artists and 116 organizations have delivered an open letter to Mayor Katie Wilson and the Seattle City Council urging amendments to the 2027 budget that would reallocate police hiring funds toward cultural infrastructure.

Amid a looming $175 million deficit, the mayor’s proposal slates a $68 million increase for the Seattle Police Department to recruit 66 officers. The coalition requests council members redirect $8 million from that proposed increase directly into the Office of Arts and Culture .

“By paying local artists to bring life to our streets, parks, and business districts, the city fostered deep community engagement,” the letter reads. “These activations increased positive foot traffic, built relationships among neighbors, and created a vibrant cultural presence everywhere from North of Downtown to the South End.”
Capitol Hill and Central District Organizations and Businesses

Signatories argue that placemaking serves as vital public safety infrastructure, pointing to a $3.6 million investment in 2025 that funded 120 grants and 80 public activations ahead of the World Cup summer.
The letter credits that initiative with curbing violence and yielding a “murder-free June.”
The requested $8 million would more than double the 2025 cultural investment to establish year-round community programming citywide.

CHS reported here on Wilson’s proposal which would wipe out a $175 million deficit without tax increases or withdrawals from city reserves. The proposal would cut roughly $50 million annually in General Fund spending by eliminating 128 positions and aligning departmental budgets with historical costs, pairing these cuts with $50 million in shuffled funding by leveraging JumpStart payroll tax revenues to cover core services and homelessness programs.
Starting next week, budget chair Dan Strauss will lead the process as council members are briefed on policy considerations before officially proposing potential amendments to the mayor’s proposal.

District 3 representative Council President Joy Hollingsworth has signaled her support for continued police and anti-crime investments, joining a call for the mayor to strengthen her public safety plan .
A final “all-day” public hearing is scheduled for November 5th .
